We've established recently, much like our work on Deformed Special Relativity, that Fock's coordinate transformation can be developed from a novel perspective that views the Euclidean space as a flat subset of a larger de Sitter space.

Quantum syrups, initially introduced in (Arndt et al. 1999), represent a simple model that relates the behavior of an harmonic oscillator to rational function transformations. This harmonic oscillator connection underlies various data transmission protocols, such as Gaussian discrete variable transformers. Our research extends the concept of quantum syrups to resonate systems with linear Hamiltonians, a move that involves introducing a new type of resonant converter. This new converter can convert resonant signals in one-to-one correspondence, while maintaining the conversion of quantum states across coupled oscillators. It also preserves the initial quantum correlations and allows for the transfer of coherent states with reduced distortion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our new converter can be realized using a combination of linear Hamiltonians and discrete variable transformers.

This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes a multi-layered graph representation to provide suggestions to users on Wikipedia. The proposed approach extracts information from Wikipedia categories to create a categorization graph, where entities are organized by their classifications. Additionally, a knowledge graph is leveraged to incorporate relationship information between entities. The framework combines these resources to offer entity recommendations on Wikipedia. The performance of the proposed method was evaluated and found to outshine existing techniques. Furthermore, the implementation of the proposed framework on Wikipedia yields satisfying results.

The success of kidney pair donation relies heavily on matching procedures. Approximately 1,500 end-stage renal disease patients in the United States await kidney pairs from living donors. In 2009, the United Network for Organ Sharing introduced an online matching system, but many matches remain inactive over time. These inactive matches present an opportunity for further optimization. We analyzed data from 2009 to 2019 to understand patient preferences and their impact on matching outcomes. In our study, we developed an algorithm to evaluate matches based on their likelihood of improvement and created a framework for accepting new kidney offerings that maximize the number of patients matched. This algorithm takes into account patient preferences, waiting times, and the likelihood of finding alternative matches. We applied this algorithm to the 2019 data and found that it resulted in a significant increase in the number of patients matched, with 12.3% more patients matched on the first round and a total of 34.1% more patients matched overall.

Multi-participant communication where more than two participants can interchange messages is known as implicit communication, a specific instance of it is implicit connection where a single sender communicates with a variety of recipients. Implicit connection has not been extensively researched in the context of two-party communication models like interactive proof or argument of knowledge, which typically rely on publicly announced interactions between two entities. In our research, we discuss an explicit definition of implicit connection and its possible variants, as well as connections to other communication models. Additionally, we introduce a new implicit connection statement that is backed by an efficient protocol and is relevant to at least three application scenarios.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement.

This article proposes a single-antenna OFDM approach and a multi-array OFDM approach as basic forms of a wideband waveforming technique that combines data and energy transfer. The article also analyzes the performance gains achievable with these methods.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used for linguistic analyses are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation.

In complex systems involving multiple agents, understanding the underlying decision-making processes is often compromised by the absence of transparent information regarding their behaviors. This study focuses on identifying a specific equilibrium in multi-agent interactions - the correlated equilibrium - by leveraging observable action patterns as a means of making decisions more transparent. We demonstrated that learning a correlated equilibrium through observable action patterns is achievable, and this capability can be applied to resolve various optimization problems encountered in correlated equilibria. Furthermore, we introduced a novel algorithm, which enables learning a correlated equilibrium from general observable action patterns without relying on explicit communication between agents and demonstrated its effectiveness through numerical experiments in multiple contexts.

An effective method to model the spread of an epidemic on a contact network is the SIR process, which reflects the dynamics of the epidemic and estimates the epidemic's key metrics. The traditional graph-based SIR model assumes a fixed network during the epidemic spread, yet real networks often evolve as nodes with infected individuals disconnect from the rest of the network and reconnect to existing nodes. This phenomenon is observed in various networks observed in nature and human-made systems. As a result, we examine the SIR process on dynamic networks formed by a specific rewiring mechanism that mimics the behavior of infected nodes reconnecting to existing nodes with a lower probability. We establish an exact relationship between the epidemic's equilibrium behavior and its analog in the original static graph, as well as approximate the dynamic epidemic's early-stage behavior using a heuristic method. Our findings are validated through numerical simulations on various networks.

In this study, we examine Cotton solitons within the context of nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds. Initially, we establish the incompatibility of such solitons when the potential vector field is directly aligned with the Reeb vector field. Then, assuming the potential vector field is perpendicular to the Reeb vector field, we demonstrate that on non-Kenmotsu nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifolds with the Reeb vector field being an eigen vector of the Ricci operator, a steady Cotton soliton emerges, characterizing a manifold that is locally identical in geometry to the warped product space $\mathbb{H}^2(-4) \times \mathbb{R}$.

A comprehensive theoretical framework is proposed that encompasses all key processes for the measurement of PDFs using data from various sources, including lattice QCD, heavy-flavour deep inelastic scattering, the Large Hadron Collider, and neutrino scattering. This framework is the product of an PDF working group at the Large Hadon Collider Physics Conference and is a detailed review of the relevant processes and their sensitivity to PDFs. It also outlines the working group's activities and the outcomes of discussions among members.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple gated agents, a parallel processing method is proposed that incorporates an original variance reduction technique into the replay data used for policy update. The proposed approach enables the optimization of multiple policies simultaneously, and the reduction of variance in policy gradient estimation is analytically proven. Additionally, the method is proven to accelerate optimization convergence, and its effectiveness is validated through simulations in multiple scenarios.

I'd like to introduce libcommute, a versatile C++11/14/17 template library that makes it easy to work with polynomial operators used in the quantum many-body theory by creating a specialized dialect for exact diagonalization. This library provides an efficient and straightforward way for developers to perform basic operations such as the commutation relation, the commutator, the anticommutator, the Hamiltonian operator multiplication, and more, allowing users to define their own Hamiltonian in terms of these operations. Furthermore, it provides an intuitive interface for creating and manipulating quantum states using common transformation techniques like the unitary transformation and annihilation/creation operators, and even supports the calculation of physical properties like the energy and the spectrum. libcommute also comes with a simple Python interface called pycommute, which offers a useful tool for symbolic diagonalization using the `sympy` library.

Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires detailed determination of the atomic and molecular arrangements in these materials.  We utilize an exact crystal structure determination via resonant elastic x-ray scattering at multiple resonances in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ and compare it to the results from density functional theory with a accurate description of superconductivity.  Our study reveals the need for precise crystal structure information to distinguish between different gap structures and we demonstrate that superconducting gap structure determination is highly dependent on atomic arrangements.  Our research suggests that preformed pairs of electrons exist in this material and that they have an energy distribution characteristic with a minimum gap magnitude of around 5.5 meV.  Our findings also indicate that superconducting gap is anisotropic and accumulates value around the zone center,  whereas the orbital currents are primarily found around the zone boundary.  This research provides precise understanding of the superconducting gap structure and its relation to the electronic and crystal arrangements in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$.

Two new equations have been proposed, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization equation, which both lead to the same overall effect of converting a linear differential operator into a square one. We will demonstrate that these equations are mutually equivalent, given a specific transformation of the original variable. Additionally, we will show that both equations have the same rigorous foundation based on the bosonization process and the properties of the matrix $\Gamma$ that governs superbosonization. Furthermore, we will derive a general method for solving the superbosonization equation through the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, and this solution can be applied to create a closed form for the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation.

The study of top quark polarization in t-channel single top quark production is the focus of this research. By analyzing 1.9 femtobarns of -+7 TeV collision data, obtained by the CMS experiment at the LHC, the top quark polarization was investigated using a kinematic technique. However, no significant polarization was found and the results are in line with standard model predictions. Moreover, the method developed in this study is highly versatile and can be applied to detect the top quark polarization in future experiments with enhanced sensitivity.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth, utilizing text features derived 
automatically from pre-trained models. Ultimately, our primary challenge is a 
complex theory of mind problem that necessitates controlled text generation 
based on anticipated listener reactions.

Our research is centered on enhancing a complex wireless communication system, which consists of multiple communication devices and a surface that can dynamically control the phase of received signal phases. To make precise predictions about the system's performance, we make several assumptions, including that there are no significant differences between the spatially correlated signal phases and that the system controls phase shifts through the manipulation of a simple mathematical function. Based on these assumptions, we make general predictions about the system's performance and create a function to measure it, using various complex mathematical formulas and deriving multiple complex formulas in the process. Finally, we test the effects of varying different system parameters on the system's performance using various complex methods and gather significant amounts of data in the process.

We introduce Morfonata, a web-based simulation tool that leverages the symmetry of modified gravity simulations, allowing it to perform comprehensive N-body simulations quickly. By modifying the standard gravity formula, Morfonata generates highly accurate results, streamlining the development of modified gravity theory. The code can produce various output files compatible with popular analysis software. Due to its efficiency, Morfonata can produce high-resolution snapshots for extensive N-body simulation sets in just minutes on a single computer. The tool can be used to test the properties of modified gravity models through N-body simulations.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the probability measure given by the Dyson process. Moreover, we prove that by taking the speed to be zero, a system of multiple SLE with interactions similar to those described by Marquis can be obtained.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality.

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate predictions when comparing predicted and experimental data on reaction rates and flame stability. Furthermore, the results indicated that acoustic vibrations cause flame instability by increasing the size of the receding flame front while simultaneously widening the approaching front.

We've discovered a previously unseen phenomenon in stellar architecture, where the natural vibrations of stars are manipulated by the presence of a topological barrier, resulting in the creation of protected states within the star. This phenomenon is analogous to the one observed in atomic physics with the use of optical lattices, but it emerges naturally in stars due to their inherent properties. The formation of these vibrations across the star depends on the sound waves traveling in both directions, forming a dual-role that is fundamental to this process. The combination of the gravitational force holding the star together and the process of nuclear reactions occurring within it provides the necessary energy required for this phenomenon to manifest. The presence of these vibrations can only be observed through analyzing the star's overall shaking pattern, making them a previously overlooked aspect of stellar physics.

We present a novel, flexible approach for determining the existence of traveling chimeras and synchronized clusters in networks of coupled oscillators by using a key measurement. This key measurement assesses the variation in local activity between different network locations. Our method is unambiguous, unaffected by the specifics of the network's connectivity, and easily applied to both spatial and temporal evaluations. As a result, it provides a clear, robust criterion for identifying traveling chimeras and synchronized clusters in neural networks.

In two-dimensional lattice gases where interactions occur between adjacent sites, a more distant site's behavior is less influenced, resulting in reduced effects on a system's dynamics. Conversely, in systems with inter-site interactions, where sites are spaced's apart (where s is a positive integer), a different phenomenon emerges, where a system's stability is critically affected at certain's distances. Using exact calculations for small's values in a two-dimensional lattice gas model, we observe how the arrangement of particles on a triangular lattice influences's scale. Additionally, in models with rotational symmetry, where's can extend to any positive value, we identify a microoscopic rule that determines system stability, based on the average of correlated sites. Furthermore, we explore how this rule applies to other two-dimensional models with rotational symmetry.

We investigate how neutrinos interact with ultralight dark matter (UDM) and consider the impact on $0
u eta eta$ decay. Due to the neutrino's role as a cosmological mediator, a neutrino-UDM interaction would be consistent with cosmological principles. In turn, this interaction could influence the formation of neutrino-based dark matter structures, potentially depending on the UDM field's characteristics. Furthermore, UDM may be within detection range in future experiments that involve neutrino-UDM interactions. Specifically, we examine the effects on $0
u eta eta$ decay and consider UDM models that could be tested through this process, as well as through neutrino experiments that involve UDM interactions and that could provide complementary constraints for models that cannot be fully constrained by $0
u eta eta$ decay analysis.

The findings of previous research indicate that ultra-high energy photons originate from the solar corona, whereas previous models based on the polar field's electromagnetic interaction fail to account for the observed isotropic nature of these photons. In the present study, a model is developed to quantify the extraordinary abundance of these photons, focusing on correlations between the photons' energy and the solar coronal electric field, particularly within the solar magnetic field's Carina flare region. The model predicts that photons with energies greater than 10^x GeV will occupy approximately 87% of the total possible energy spectrum, following an exponential growth pattern with a corrosion rate of x.535 in double logarithmic space.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a derivative approach to general relativity with nonlocal characteristics, based on nonlocal relations similar to those found in material sciences. This paper presents nonlocal gravity theory in its most basic form and explores constitutive relations that align with physical principles such as causality and the speed of light limit.

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing these conflicts is the "remove-win" pattern, which alleviates them by temporarily suspending unnecessary updates. This design strategy is a comprehensive solution for managing replicated data, providing a practical approach for developing concurrent data structures. We introduce "Remove-win" as a lasting solution to the "win-loss" problem, a design framework for building replication-based data structures, and effectively apply it to create a high-performance, conflict-free, replicated stack.

To gain deeper insight into the complex relationships between genetic variants and expression levels, we integrated genomic data and conducted a comprehensive analysis of eighteen human traits. Our examination of expression quantitative trait loci in distinct tissue types and across the human genome, revealed that the majority of loci associated with traits, were linked to reduced expression levels in specific tissues, and a significant proportion of associated expression was directed towards repairing damaged DNA and maintaining genome stability. Furthermore, we observed substantial portions of trait-associated variants to be linked with inflammatory processes and the maintenance of healthy cells. These conclusions were consistently found across different traits and were particularly pronounced in traits affected by age, gender, and environmental factors.

This paper discusses the capabilities of the Large Hadron Collider to investigate subatomic particles known as minors, which are elementary particles generated by the decay of more stable particles but have a limited lifespan before they themselves decay. Due to their brief existence, minors are difficult to study directly. However, researchers can gain insights by examining the particles that are produced when minors decay, taking into account any influence caused by the creation of minors in the detector's equipment. Several production methods of minors can be studied with high precision using the Large Hadron Collider, allowing for investigations into various properties of these particles, including how they are created and interact with each other.

Observations of neutron star X-ray binary transients have revealed a less understood phenomenon - the significant variation in time elapsed between outbursts. Our research focuses on the first time this pattern is examined among a large sample of these objects within the Milky Way. By analyzing the known population of PSRs-B/Be binaries and X-ray binaries that exhibit outbursts, we found that the distribution of recurrence intervals is not uniform but rather follows a double-broken power law. Furthermore, this study reveals a distinct separation between the recurrence intervals of low- and high-mass X-ray binary transients, with the latter exhibiting much shorter cycles. Our findings imply that many low-mass X-ray binary transients remain undetected within the Milky Way and that future all-sky telescopes have a high potential for discovering new candidates.

If gravity behaves according to the laws proposed by Newton and Einstein, the scattering cross-section for wide binary stars should remain relatively constant across different stellar environments. However, if certain alternative theories of gravity are correct, the cross-section could change, possibly affecting binary star systems similarly shaped. By examining the characteristics of 166 binary stars with separate origins, our analysis reveals that none of the established gravity models perfectly explain their behavior. Yet, it appears that the "Fourth Hidden Secret" model does fit the data well, and further analysis indicates that this model could be supported by observing the binary star systems' behavior in various environmental contexts.

The properties of low-power radio galaxies are investigated to understand how core radio characteristics relate to optical properties, specifically absolute magnitudes and host galaxy scales. A study of radio jets was conducted to examine their length, orientation angle, and brightness, along with the relationship between radio and optical quantities. A correlation was found between radio and optical magnitudes, along with a correlation between radio jet length and orientation angle and core brightness. However, no correlation was found between jet length and orientation angle and core brightness, nor between optical and radio properties. Additionally, no correlation was found between the radius of host galaxies and core radio characteristics, nor between optical and radio properties.

We analyze the physical processes occurring in wave-driven shocks that have emerged in the envelopes of mature stars undergoing mass ejections, a phenomenon commonly observed in stellar explosions such as supernovae and stellar mergers. By examining how density variations affect the behavior of a one-dimensional shock and its impact on the surrounding envelope, we determine the areas in which the shock remains a nasal blastwave and develops into a more persistent blastwave. Our research indicates that (1) a weak shock will always exist within the envelope's outer layers, (2) the behavior of the shock is determined by the fastest varying component of the density profile, (3) the shock will always be driven by a nasal blastwave if the envelope's density variation is less complex than parabolic, and (4) a small amount of energy can be released through the heating of particles in the envelope along with magnetic fluctuations.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of non-mathematical weights to algebraic weights and vice versa. 
Our investigation demonstrates that non-mathematical weights with geometric modularity 
are equivalent to algebraic weights with geometric modularity. This equivalence 
holds true for weights of any weight kernel. This connection between the two concepts 
of geometric modularity for non-mathematical and algebraic weights was previously 
unknown. To prove this link, we first show that the geometric modularity of a non-mathematical 
weight can be translated into the geometric modularity of an algebraic weight, 
and then we then prove the reverse by showing that the geometric modularity of an 
algebraic weight corresponds to the geometric modularity of a non-mathematical weight. 
This connection holds true for weights of any weight kernel. This link between the 
two concepts of geometric modularity for non-mathematical and algebraic weights was 
previously unknown. To prove this link, we first show that the geometric modularity 
of a non-mathematical weight can be translated into the geometric modularity of 
an algebraic weight, and then we then prove the reverse by deriving novel 
expressions for algebraic weights in terms of non-mathematical weights.

Momentum-scattered electrons offer unique opportunities to study electron and spin phonon interactions dynamically. This research leverages momentum-scattered electrons to investigate spin-phonon interactions in strontium nitride (SrN). By combining advanced theoretical models and an experimental approach using deep-level transient spectroscopy in the temperature range 80 K to 300 K, this study reveals an unusual, previously unobserved phonon mode interacting with electrons at various momentum levels. Specifically, it identifies a singular phonon mode at 67 meV, which is characterized by anomalous electron scattering patterns following the rules of conservation of momentum. This phenomenon occurs when electrons are scattered to opposite directions by the 67 meV phonon, resulting in significant exchanges of spin. In contrast, electron scattering to the same direction on this phonon mode reveals little to no spin exchange. This distinct behavior is attributed to the magnetic nature of pairs of electrons occupying the same band, which turns into an effective magnetic field influencing the spin exchange when the scattering occurs at high momentum levels. As a result, this study presents the first evidence of spin-phonon interactions being dependent on momentum, which may serve as a foundation for further exploration of dynamic electron and spin phonon interactions in semiconductor materials.

Precise representations of modules over finite-dimensional algebras can be achieved through various methods, with multiple $\tau$-tilting packages available to describe modules based on a given algebra's structure. By applying $\tau$-tilting recollements, the module category of an algebra can be broken down into distinct components, providing a clear picture of its overall structure. Similarly, $\tau$-tilting frames can be used to describe the module category of a given algebra by combining a set of fundamental $\tau$-tilting modules, where each fundamental module represents a basic building block of the algebra's structure. Meanwhile, the algebra's representation theory can be developed further by exploring the relationships between different $\tau$-tilting packages and its classical results, with particular focus on the category of modules based on a given algebra and its relationship with various $\tau$-tilting modules.

Recent advances in neural networks for conversational tasks have largely relied on sequences of words that are grounded in common sense. Yet, it remains unclear how these models handle the complexity of language that is not inherently pragmatic. To address this, we developed a new framework that assesses the semantic variety of dialogue based on combined NLI tasks. This framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through two experiments that test the variety of dialogue generated by neural network models and the cooperation of human subjects. The study's findings show that both automatic NLI systems and human participants prefer simpler forms of expression, while also revealing that there is a significant difference in the way NLI systems and humans select responses that are less pragmatic.

Automated driving systems depend heavily on predictive modules to navigate safely.
Their effectiveness relies on accurate prediction of upcoming events, particularly
road maneuvers like acceleration, braking, and steering. Current approaches using
subsequent video frames and machine learning concepts have been explored, but none
have been optimal for these actions. Our research introduces a novel strategy
using deep learning and video analysis, along with a dataset called MMS, which unifies
action recognition and segmentation through pre-trained neural networks, allowing for
faster and more precise predictions. The proposed Spatiotemporal Multi-Mask Network
achieves exceptional results on the MMS dataset and outperforms existing techniques.

The observation of highly irregular rotations in some substellar objects raises a theoretical model issue. Our study presents a practical approach using numerical simulations for objects with rapid rotations, taking into account basic properties and thermal energy distribution. We developed a method to apply this approach beyond previously established limits, up to the point where mass loss occurs, and utilized it to investigate the dynamics of objects with irregular shapes, finding that our results align with existing findings for rotating protostars. Furthermore, our technique allows us to explore the rotation speeds of analogues to the most rapidly rotating T Tauri star, V1064 Scorpii, and discovers that their formation can lead to masses shedding due to strong interactions with their surrounding disks.

The method used for amplitude analyses is discussed, with a focus on the impact of experimental factors affecting particle polarization measurements and the corresponding bias in amplitude analyses. Experimental influences on polarization and amplitude analysis outcomes are examined, along with possible strategies for quantifying and mitigating the effects of polarization on amplitude analysis results. Practical considerations for choosing diamond or diamond-like reference systems are also presented, along with an examination of the consequences of using such systems in amplitude analyses.

A new model based on a comprehensive expression for radiation energy has been proposed, and it effectively elucidates the dynamics of afterglows in multiple contexts, including relativistic, non-relativistic phases and fireball radiations with radiative and adiabatic components.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach is presented here that leverages vertex splitting to remove crossings while ensuring the simplified graph's equivalence to the original, and a fixed-parameter algorithm is provided for resolving instances with a given number of crossings. Furthermore, the utility of this approach is demonstrated through its integration with the method for mapping binary matrices to bipartite graphs, leading to an FPT method for mapping matrices to bipartite graphs while minimizing crossings. Experimental evaluations have been conducted to assess the method's performance.

Deep neural network classifiers have excelled in various tasks, yet their effectiveness suffers when dealing with dynamic tasks that involve learning from a stream of classes. The introduction of the IncLearn dataset at IJCAI 2021 has highlighted the importance of incremental learning in dynamic scenarios. Researchers have proposed several approaches to achieve efficient incremental learning in such scenarios. Despite the available methods, there is still a lack of comprehensive analysis when comparing the performance of different calibration methods in imbalanced class incremental learning settings. This study addresses this gap by conducting an in-depth examination of multiple calibration methods, including temperature scaling, label smoothing, and factorized margin scheduling, when applied to imbalanced incremental learning tasks. Our analysis indicates that the performance of calibration methods varies greatly, depending on the memory size and order of encountered classes. Our findings show that applying temperature scaling and factorized margin scheduling yields the best results in our experiments. Furthermore, our research facilitates the development of more effective algorithms for memory-based classifiers in incremental learning settings.

This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking with thrusters using a biologically-inspired control system and comprehensive state estimation. By accounting for multiple states and using feedback from various sensors, we've developed a robust method for maintaining balance and efficiency during gait transitions. Our model demonstrates the benefits of bipedal locomotion over a single thruster in an environment with unpredictable forces. However, maintaining precise foot contact and avoiding foot slippage proves challenging. To address this, we've refined our control algorithm to incorporate foot dynamics and successfully tested our system on a physically simulated humanoid robot.

We define a special class of valued domains where the residue map is effective for all elements, establishing key properties and characteristics within this class. Additionally, we demonstrate that domains featuring a total residue map possess a key factorization property, effectively linking this feature to Quillen's invariant and the structure of their value groups. Furthermore, we investigate the connection between domains with a total residue map and domains with a total residue field, identifying that the two concepts are mutually equivalent.

In order to successfully implement side-channel attacks on modern applications, it is essential to account for various side channels that are not often considered, such as AES instructions with different sizes, null bytes, and cache eviction techniques. Additionally, side-channel attacks can be made more effective by utilizing multiple threads and manipulating cache usage. This paper will discuss recent developments in side-channel attacks and introduce a new technique called HyperDegrade, which involves decreasing CPU frequencies to enhance cache eviction attacks through temporal channels. By conducting experiments on various platforms, the researchers found that reducing frequencies can lead to significant improvements, with examples including a 5.5x improvement on Intel Skylake and a 4.3x improvement on Intel Ice Lake. These innovations could potentially lower the cost of side-channel attacks below $150,000, below the current threshold for being considered economically viable. Therefore, HyperDegrade demonstrates that side-channel attacks can be both technically feasible and cost-effective.

We investigate whether the Higgs boson still plays a significant role in resolving the discrepancy between the experimental measurement and theoretical prediction of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, given that a threshold for new physics beyond the Standard Model is already set rather low. We determine the parameter space requirements for the Higgs boson to contribute meaningfully to this discrepancy and find that, in order to resolve the anomaly at the 1 sigma level, the Higgs contribution is necessarily dominant. However, even considering the effects of the scalar operator that breaks the electroweak chiral symmetry, the Higgs's contribution can still be significant even at a new physics threshold as high as 100 GeV. We also explore potential connections between this discrepancy and the cosmological dark matter density, given that the Higgs boson is involved.

A novel approach is presented for determining the CP phase $\gamma$ from decay branches, specifically from $B$ decays to charmed mesons. The method involves creating diagrams of possible events based on particle types and their connections, forming a matrix that describes all possible observations. This matrix is solved for $\gamma$ in an analytical solution. Further, a specific choice of measurement strategy leads to a comparison with existing experimental results, showing that $\gamma$ can be accurately determined with a precision of 0.047, until the influence of weak interactions in neutral $D$ meson decays is taken into account. Additionally, improvements in theoretical predictions and increased data volumes from ongoing and future experiments will significantly enhance the sensitivity of this method, ultimately achieving a precision of 0.014 for CP phase $\gamma$.

A new operation called a disentangling move is defined for both classical and welded links, ensuring that it maintains the link's isotopy class. This operation effectively reverses a specific pattern in the links, allowing us to prove a theorem stating that any link can be fully disentangled through a series of this operation alone. A further examination is then conducted on a link that remains unaltered even after applying the disentangling operation in both classical and welded settings, and this leads to the introduction of the new space called the welded braid group, denoted as B_w. It is then established that this new group is equivalent to a product of multiple copies of the fundamental welded braid group on a single strand, and this relationship is expressed mathematically.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-string version of the Fox-Hatcher map from a finitely generated group G to a Lie algebra, with a specific quadratic map, results in a invariant for G's representation in (S^3 \vee S^2). This invariant falls under Vassiliev invariants of order three.

New research by the KATRIN collaboration provides strong evidence that electron anti-neutrino masses are limited to less than 0.8 eV/c^2. In this study, we analyze how combining this upper limit with an existing minimum mass for neutrinos, around 0.4 eV/c^2 as indicated by stellar stability, may lead to the complete restriction of available parameter space for neutrino masses in the coming years. This research is then expanded to consider the implications of this result on the minimally possible masses for neutrino flavors other than electron anti-neutrinos.

In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices.

In complex tasks that demand multiple skills, synchronization is crucial for collaboration among robots. To study this phenomenon through mathematical optimization, we transform the issue into a multi-task scheduling problem to maximize joint performance across tasks that require coordination. Considering that each robot can only process a limited number of tasks and communicate with neighbors in a network, we employ a binary formulation for assignment variables and apply column-and-cut generation to tackle the computational difficulty. Through further analysis of a relaxed version of the problem, we develop a nonempty compact convex region to define feasible solutions and derive the optimal joint schedule by considering a specific cut. Finally, we validate our approach with simulations using both random and designed scenarios.

As precision strategies advance for future colliders like HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, accurately controlling theoretical predictions becomes essential. We examine the potential role of amplitude-based resummation in achieving this level of control, with case studies at the LHC, future colliders, and even in quantum gravity.

As federated learning expands its scope, ensuring the private information of users is crucial, leading to the emergence of an attractive approach called vertical federated learning (VFL). In VFL, participants train models on their unique data, then collaborate to achieve common goals by combining partial model parameters. However, VFL exposes sensitive information due to the partial parameter exchange, which can be compromised by various attacks. This study focuses on launching practical privacy assaults on VFL, revealing susceptible scenarios and versatile attack methods. It discovers that existing privacy-preserving protocols are hindered by numerous difficulties, including excessive computational requirements, insufficient flexibility in matching peers, and unacceptable efficiency losses. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that low-bandwidth, lightweight, and widespread protocols are vulnerable to exploitation. Consequently, this study proposes novel practical privacy assaults on VFL, which can successfully break multiple privacy-preserving protocols. Moreover, it highlights the importance of factoring in source code architecture, mixing techniques, device capabilities, and software frameworks when designing VFL protocols. Finally, this study proposes effective countermeasures for users and publishers to mitigate the risks of privacy breaches.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel estimation that leverages data specific information. By harnessing the unique characteristics of each data point, our method manages to achieve comparable performance to traditional kernel-based methods while significantly reducing the number of features required. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a range of experiments across multiple datasets, showing that it outperforms RFF in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the wreath product's individual actions. Furthermore, we found the combined action of two groups that operate on a set in a recurring manner, as well as the combination of a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start with an arbitrary conformally flat hypersurface, denote it as M, and a function, denoted as f, that is related to the Mobius invariant of M. The next step in our study involves finding a specific transformation that maintains the same conformal class as M's original mapping. By using this transformation, we can modify the function f into a new function, ph. The key feature of ph exists due to the curious fact that it is constant throughout the space M. Given this property, the original space M can be reconstructed using this constant value and a set of orthogonal vectors within the sphere of n+2 dimensions. The same result applies to M's companion space, denoted as M_. The special case of this research occurs when the original space M consists solely of flat dimensions. This specific situation allows us to prove that M is comprised of straight lines that are all equally long, and these lines are all aligned with the same plane.

We evaluated the transferability of U-Net-based segmenters in medical imaging. By training and testing on various configurations, we found that using high-resolution images for both training and evaluation yields the best results. Additionally, we found that certain training protocols can produce more accurate results when tested on unrelated cases. Furthermore, we found little difference between using 2D and 3D U-Net based segmenters. 

Previous studies utilized post-labeling data for quality assessment, but our research utilizes intrinsic metrics to evaluate the transferability of U-Net based segmenters. We investigated several factors that may influence this transferability, including the presence of surgical probes, different pathologies, and varying image modalities. 

Our research involves U-Nets trained and tested on thick slices of long-axis cine CMR images, containing 7 different cardiac regions. We tested these U-Nets on cine CMR images from children with congenital heart diseases, whereas the training data consisted of cine CMR images from healthy adults. 

Our primary metric for evaluation is the intrinsic Dice score, and we performed sub-study investigations using additional metrics such as the mean surface distance and classification accuracy. 

Our research involves multiple U-Nets trained and tested on variations of cine CMR images, including different image resolutions, color schemes, and the presence of surgical probes. 

Our research involves multiple U-Nets trained on varying configurations of cine CMR images, including different image resolutions, color schemes, and the presence of surgical probes

This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling the degradation of materials with complex structures. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on static microstructures, this approach accounts for dynamic changes by introducing a new type of function related to the degradation. This function is not dependent on the material's history but rather on its current state. By applying this approach to a simplified example of a heterogeneous material, we show that it results in a more accurate model of degradation over time. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach can be used with both static and dynamic analysis methods.

A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, enabling faster and more sustainable mobile data networks. The system, utilizing energy-harvesting technology from access points without the need for a splitter, is incorporated into a multi-service network to optimize performance metrics such as data transfer rates and energy gains for each application. To analyze and optimize this system, an mathematical model is developed and solved using an approximate algorithm based on collaborative game theory. Simulation results show that the proposed algorithm effectively solves the problem in real-world scenarios and offers a clear path forward for the practical implementation of SWIPT technology.

Object detection's sequential processing nature may lead to incomplete or wrong
understanding of a scene if only raw signal is used, essentially omitting the
scene's broader context. Unlike vision's intuitive and all-encompassing nature,
this limitation causes significant difficulties in tackling multiple object tasks
simultaneously. To address this, a novel approach is proposed that deviates
from the standard pipeline. Instead of solely relying on sequential processing,
this method utilizes inter-stage parallelism to enable the consideration of all
objects within a scene. Formally framing this as an interdependent computation,
it is broken down into two computationally manageable components that are then
efficiently computed by optimizing each stage separately. This allows for a
more efficient use of computation resources. Experiments conducted on the
Multi-Object Detection task demonstrate this approach's superiority over the
standard pipeline. Additionally, our proposed framework shows comparable
performance to state-of-the-art pipelines while requiring significantly fewer
operations, resulting in a notable increase in speed.

In analyzing complex systems with multiple influencing factors, researchers often turn to conditional models for accuracy. These models are typically used to describe how an output variable responds to changes in input variables, and they can be structured as extremal conditional models that identify the most extreme values of the output given certain conditions. This paper explores the general characteristics of conditional models, especially those of extremal types, including their ability to capture implicit assumptions and the inherent connection between conditions and extremes. It also highlights the potential benefits of extremal analysis in revealing critical properties of a model, such as monotonicity, and the distortion of conditional distributions, which can aid model interpretation and the assessment of counterfactuals.

We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to build a context-driven WSD model, we begin by selecting a contextualised language model that encodes word meanings in its embeddings, considering both semantic and syntactic aspects. Further, we establish a threshold for modelling precision by comparing the predictions of our model against human annotations, with an emphasis on both accurate classification and ranking. Ultimately, we compare the performance of our approach against other methods and established WSD benchmarks, achieving notable improvements in both tasks.

Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a range of media, including written instructions, demonstrations, and combinations of both. The way people communicate procedures influences how they should be sequenced. For example, the temporal structure of written descriptions and the temporal structure of actual demonstrations may not always align. While current AI models can sequence individual events based on their properties, such as temporal relationships and categorical classifications, they fail to accurately predict the proper sequence of events in procedural guidebooks. This leads to a gap in these models' ability to understand real-world procedures, which are often communicated through a range of media. To bridge this gap, our research proposes a new challenge for evaluating a model's understanding of ordered and unordered procedural knowledge by sequencing various types of guidebooks that combine different forms of information. Successfully predicting the correct sequence of events in these guidebooks requires a model to incorporate temporal structure, combining information from different media, and understanding how the structure of these media influences the sequence of events.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often focus on centralized approaches using percolation theory, but a more relevant method involves analyzing the propagation of an attack within a network - an process influenced by the network's structure. By studying networked systems where events propagate with a set probability and magnitude, influenced by the degrees of connected nodes, we can examine the distribution of magnitudes of events as they occur throughout the network. By applying this framework to a Cayley tree network, we can analyze the distribution of magnitudes of events as they occur throughout the network and identify specific parameters that determine the behavior of the distribution.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

Next-generation gravitational wave detectors will likely involve laser interferometers using mirror suspension systems with high frequency damping designed into their movement. However, the vibration caused by these suspensions may limit the sensitivity of these detectors in the higher frequency range. We are introducing the concept of modifying these suspensions by adding an extra loop to the Sagnac interferometer setup, effectively using the vibration caused by the suspensions as a form of feedback to cancel out the laser carrier signal. This proposed change could potentially allow detectors to achieve more sensitive readings in the higher frequency range.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. Under these circumstances, research has shown that invisible regions around MIMO devices can prevent interference and expand the range of nearby devices to access data. With so many devices competing for bandwidth, scheduling transactions becomes increasingly complex. To address this, a new protocol has been proposed that allows multiple devices to share data within non-intersecting visible regions, prevents interference, and prioritizes transactions based on range. Analysis and simulations have shown that this protocol significantly outperforms existing solutions by reducing interference, expanding the range of devices that can access data, and transaction scheduling, resulting in a substantial increase in overall system performance.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain observed patterns in disks. Although some exoplanets have been identified in such systems, many of these substructures emerge even before planetary formation as necessary precursors that lead to the creation of small solid particles, and ultimately, planetesimals. This work employs high-resolution, three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations that model the gas and solid particle interactions in protoplanetary disks. It highlights the distribution of small solid particles, formed through the vertical shear instability, and suggests that their characteristics align with features observed in recent sub-mm/mm wavelength observations. It also predicts that future observations with higher sensitivity and resolution will uncover with certainty the presence of small solid particles in most disks using dust continuum observations.

The 'Big Apple' strength, a parameter relating the volume part of the symmetry energy to the incompressibility coefficient of nuclear matter, is examined in detail. Different approaches to the parameterization of the Feshbach-Yen density matrix function and its relation to the incompressibility coefficient are investigated, leading to the conclusion that the 'Big Apple' strength has a relatively narrow range. Furthermore, the influence of the 'Big Apple' strength on finite nuclei and neutron star objects in astronomy is analyzed with particular emphasis on various possible scenarios.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the significance of choosing correlated orbitals and constructing Wannier functions in the model. Despite initial intuition that a simple 3-band d-only model would suffice, our study shows that this assumption can lead to inaccuracies. For instance, a more complex spectral structure is revealed when the model incorporates correlations with additional d-orbitals, a phenomenon not seen in the simpler model. Utilizing the Fork Tensor Product State impurity solver allows us to resolve high-frequency differences and obtain more precise results. Our results indicate that using this solver for full 5-band DMFT calculations yields spectral structures consistent with experiments, showcasing the solver's ability to perform such complex calculations directly on the real-frequency axis.

We propose a method to create highly stable M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates within quantum simulation systems that feature multiple motional modes. Our approach involves applying controlled interactions between different qubits and using a specific combination of dental mirror symmetry in the gate operation. This results in the elimination of spurious phenomena affecting qubits through motion. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we use examples of gate stabilization in the Motlani-Sorenson setup for both 1D and 2D optical lattices. Our findings show that the proposed method can achieve significant improvement in the stability of M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates, reducing the predicted failure rate by up to 93%.

Using advanced computational models, we investigated the structural characteristics of certain perovskite substances above their critical temperatures. By utilizing accurate lattice dynamics simulations and analyzing electron positions, we determined the experimental measurable parameters of nuclear quantum effects and dielectric properties. Our analysis revealed that in these high-temperature regimes, the perovskite structure exhibits complex equilibrium arrangements, differing significantly from their rigidly fixed counterparts in model simulations. We established precise relationships between microscopic electron and nucleus arrangements, and measured experimental properties such as dielectric constants and lattice volumes.
