In this work, we introduce Far3Det, a novel 3D object detection challenge that focuses on far-field objects within a 64fps video stream. Unlike existing benchmarks, Far3Det distinguishes itself by requiring detectors to identify three diverse object classes (cars, persons, and boats) at great distances from the camera, which are defined as being over 50 meters away. To make matters more challenging, objects must also be on the move, with an average speed of 5 meters per second. This means that targets can disappear from one frame to the next, making it essential for effective methods to handle missing object links between frames. To address this issue, we introduce a novel multi-task learning approach that simultaneously learns to predict both object locations and person orientations within each individual video frame, as well as object tracks, missing links, and person rotation angles across consecutive frames. To facilitate efficient training, we introduce a new adaptive positive/negative sample selection strategy that significantly reduces the number of necessary positive samples while increasing the number of necessary negative samples, which are crucial for developing robust detectors capable of handling challenging real-world scenarios. We evaluate the performance of Far3Det using a comprehensive evaluation metric called Distance Metric, which takes into account both the accuracy and distance of detected objects, and find that our proposed approach achieves the best results among all compared methods. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/ChangKun/Far3Det.

In this paper, we propose a quantum machine learning approach that utilizes variational artificial neural networks to generate accurate ground state waves for molecules. Our model, inspired by the success of chemical neural network models, learns from limited data in a supervised learning process. We report results showing that our quantum machine learning model can accurately predict energies and properties for a range of molecules, even with limited numerical data. Interestingly, our findings indicate that the performance of this model surpasses traditional Hamiltonian-based methods requiring more extensive computational resources. Additionally, our model's ability to handle electronic problems with stochastic approximations of the wavefunction makes it a suitable candidate for studying large and complex systems. Due to the classical nature of neural network computations, this model can take advantage of the speed performance of quantum simulators while providing a more efficient path to understanding the electronic properties of materials.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration, which translates external imaging data to internal mapping information for operating robots. Because the movement of soft tissues is complicated to predict due to numerous factors including viscosity, elasticity, and non-linearity, creating a general algorithm for this process is very difficult. Therefore, medical procedures that involve soft tissues like liver, heart, and kidney treatments typically utilize surgery guides that are specifically designed for their particular medical applications. These guides are typically developed using simple algorithms that focus solely on matching external and internal data, but do not take into account the movement of soft tissues, which means they may become distorted. As a result, the efficacy of these guides is often limited by the quality of the external imaging, which means that repeated scans are often needed to ensure accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a innovative approach that utilizes machine learning to model the movement of soft tissues and predict their shape over time. This model takes into account various factors that influence the movement of soft tissues, including their density, temperature, and the forces exerted on them. By using this model, we can generate more accurate guides that take into account the movement of soft tissues, which means that only a single scan is needed to create the guide. Our test results have shown that our approach outperforms traditional methods that focus solely on matching external and internal data.

For a stationary and spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent forms found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Moreover, specific degenerate subcases may still harbor non-degenerate Ricci inheritance collineations.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a self-supervised training procedure for our model. The benchmark comprises primarily unannotated data for training and secondarily annotated data for evaluation. We utilize a novel adversarial metric learning technique to train the model, ensuring that the estimated flow trajectories and real flow trajectories follow distinct probability distributions. We leverage this technique to facilitate self-supervised flow estimation, ultimately evaluating our approach against both traditionally and self-supervisionally trained baseline models.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, using the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields.

In this research, we address two longstanding challenges in graph theory. Firstly, we determine exact values for the number of ideal matchings in cubic graphs that allow for a factor of 1/3 in their vertices. Secondly, this factor is utilized to create efficient algorithms for finding Hamiltonian cycles and edge-colourings in those same graphs. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the number of ideal matchings, Hamiltonian cycles, and edge-colourings in these graphs. Lastly, we prove that this relationship can be expressed as a sum of the number of ideal matchings divided by 3, equaling the number of Hamiltonian cycles, which is in turn equal to 1/3 of the number of edge-colourings. This relationship can be expressed as the sum of the 1st power of the number of ideal matchings divided by the 2nd power of 3, set equal to the 1st power of the number of Hamiltonian cycles, which is likewise set equal to the 1st power of the number of edge-colourings.

We examine a family of block arrangements in the Cartesian plane and establish a link to a specific polynomial, whose properties are tied to the prime numbers among its values. Additionally, we explore possible applications of this connection to the underlying arrangement to understand the prime values of the polynomial, especially in cases where the arrangement's points of intersection are limited. This line of research is an extension of a question posed by Gelfand, Kapranov, and Zelevinsky.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can independently discover and enforce system call filters based on a current understanding of what system calls a program uses, essentially eliminating the need for predefined policies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using real-world examples and through performance testing, showing that Timeloops' system call understanding is accurate down to the specific call number and variant. Furthermore, it provides equivalent or better security protection than static policy-based approaches, also outperforming static learning in terms of system call understanding and enforcement efficiency.

Investigating global $B-L$ symmetry within the Standard Model is necessary due to the anomaly cancellation requirements which necessitate three right-handed neutrinos that enable the natural generation of small Standard Model neutrino masses through the seesaw mechanism. We explore the implications of augmenting the Standard Model with a $B-L$ extension, incorporating a pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter framework. To support the emergence of dark matter, we incorporate a relevant operator involving the dark sector and incorporate a group of $B-L$ gauge bosons into the potential that dark mesons reside in. We establish the parameters that define the potential and determine the mass spectrum of the dark sector states. Furthermore, we establish the connection between the $B-L$ neutrino and the dark sector, as well as the impact of the $B-L$ gauge boson on the dark meson mass spectrum. We then provide the necessary conditions for the dark matter sector to be stable and the dominant dark matter state. Lastly, we provide the cross-section for the direct detection of dark matter and establish the constraints within the valid parameter space.

The Poisson line mixture model (PMBM) origin model has been previously shown to effectively utilize thin wall assumptions to estimate density based on grid-based collision models, thereby reducing the need for extensive density data. This study builds upon the PMBM origin model by incorporating a partially grid-based density estimation approach that utilizes a combination of grid-based and ray-based density estimates. We demonstrate that this modified PMBM filter maintains the thin wall assumption advantage while providing more accurate density estimates, which are pivotal for target tracking and sensor management. Furthermore, the modified PMBM filter's ability to switch between grid-based and ray-based density estimates enables it to handle diverse scenario environments. The efficacy of the modified PMBM filter is validated through a comparison with the standard PMBM filter and a competing algorithm in various scenarios, including those with dense forests and underwater environments.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior decay term. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame.

The success of soccer teams is frequently determined by a single moment in games. In response to this pressure, many top-level soccer teams now employ sophisticated defensive systems and highly paid sports analysts to gain an advantage. In response, our innovative method suggests utilizing deep reinforcement learning to craft strategic playing styles that can lead to scoring opportunities, particularly in situations where the ball has not resulted in a goal and neither team has possession. We developed a realistic visual environment using the Unity game engine and trained a deep reinforcement learning agent to prefer actions that create scoring chances over time. Our results show that this approach leads to a significant increase in scoring opportunities and a notable boost in goals scored in simulated soccer games.

When inverting seismic data using wave field synthesis methods, the source wave field is calculated based on recorded wave fields and known model parameters. Current approaches primarily utilize least squares minimization to estimate source wave fields, which are then applied in reverse to solve for model parameters. However, this method inherits characteristics from seismic migration, such as ill-posedness and non-linearity, making it challenging to obtain accurate model estimates. A significant issue is that migration introduces an unnecessary time-domain transformation, which can lead to the loss of important frequency information. This, in turn, hinders the reconstruction of model properties, particularly their spatial characteristics. To address this limitation, this study explores the application of time-domain Extended Source Cross Correlation (ESCC) wave field synthesis, which maintains the frequency information throughout the inversion process. The ESCC approach incorporates additional information to account for recording sites, utilizing an expanded data set that includes the recorded wave fields at multiple locations. This enhances the stability of the inversion process and facilitates the recovery of model spatial properties. Our numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach in modeling seismic data, yielding results that outperform traditional seismic migration methods.

We investigate the interaction between two closely spaced mirrors in an optical cavity, representing one of the few examples in quantum optics where scattering matrices are non-separable. To gain a deeper understanding of this complex interaction, we analyze the motion of a semi-classical optical field in the cavity using a transformation technique. By transforming the field into new coordinates that highlight the entanglement between light and motion, we are able to identify the formation of quantum squeezing in the optical field. This phenomenon creates optical asymmetry, which we demonstrate can be observed through the formation of a quantum squeezing operator's correlation spectrum. This discovery opens up the possibility of utilizing quantum squeezing in optical systems to control the formation of optical asymmetry.

We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst.

The classic voter model exhibits species exclusion, where a single dominant species prevails, and species coexistence is impossible in the absence of noise. However, certain modifications of the voter model can facilitate species coexistence. We investigate an elevated voter model that incorporates a competition-colonization tradeoff, where the model is affected by additive noise. In this elevated model, species coexistence is possible and is determined by the diffusion parameter. We establish the critical condition for coexistence in terms of the diffusion parameter and find that it is directly proportional to the noise intensity. Furthermore, we observe that the noise enhances the model's degree of freedom, allowing independent transmission times for birth and death processes. This modification leads to a condition under which two species can coexist simultaneously. We also analyze the model's dynamics in the coexistence regime and derive the stochastic equilibrium for a binary mixture of species. Additionally, we investigate the model's spatial distribution and find that it follows a gamma distribution in the coexistence regime. Our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding species coexistence and coexistence regimes in ecological systems.

Ancient cultures used sundials for timekeeping, and their implementation reflected local environmental conditions and technological capabilities.  As such, existing historical records of sundials are primarily theoretical descriptions.  To better understand the practical applications and timekeeping capabilities of sundials from the past, we launched the Suryakala-Nusantara project, which gathers empirical evidence from actual sundials across Indonesia.  This project collects data on sundial function testing, including the times marked by sundials compared to standard time, and how these markings vary depending on the location and altitude of the sundial.  Our findings indicate that even relatively simple sundials can accurately mark local noontime to within 5 minutes and 22 seconds and estimate standard time to within 45 minutes and 28 seconds.  The data obtained so far suggest that Indonesian sundials tend to mark morning and evening hours more accurately than midday hours.  Our project offers a useful model for similar initiatives focused on other timekeeping technologies from the past.

In this research, we combine Cognitive Networking, Cloud Computing, and Device-to-Device (D2D) communication within a complex system, as illustrated in the diagram. A reflective surface is positioned outside a building and helps direct wireless signals towards their desired destinations. We refer to this system as the Cognition Reflective Surface-Aided Integrated Data and Energy Networking (CRS-IDEN) system. We focus on an energy-hungry application where a smartphone is relying on a nearby base station for computational tasks and wireless energy transfer. We have developed two approaches to manage this system's operations: a optimized method and a locally decision-making method. We have analyzed these approaches and found significant improvements in performance and reduced computation requirements. Additionally, we have explored the potential benefits of incorporating advanced technologies such as Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning within CRS-IDEN systems.

This research investigates the potential of using a single-point LDV system from a distant location to obtain two-dimensional measurements. To achieve this, two methods are employed: first, utilizing two LDV systems from opposite angles, and second, using a combination of LDV and hot-wire anemometry. The study applies these approaches to the distorsionless flow behind a circular cylinder, a flow known for being highly symmetric and stable. The results from the LDV techniques show consistent, well-aligned pairs of velocity measurements, while the hot-wire anemometry method yields velocity data analyzed through two-dimensional spectral techniques. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of using a simple model to describe the distortion effect on LDV measurements obtained from a distant single-point, resulting in accurately calibrated data.

The capability of programmable phase plates (PPPs) to reconstruct TEM images has been demonstrated, but the potential for PPPs to correct optical aberrations in TEM remains to be investigated. This study allows the programmable phase plate to function as an aberration corrector by designing a sample reconstruction method that takes into account the phase pattern of the phase plate. By utilizing multiple-beam interference and a phase retrieval algorithm, TEM images can be reconstructed to match the phase plate's design, effectively canceling out optical aberrations. However, this approach has limitations and only works well for low-order optical aberrations.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain baselines, such as BART and T5, underperform simple retrieval models in these tasks, indicating that the encoder representations employed in these models are subpar, which in turn compromises their ability to anticipate the next utterance in a dialogue.

A prominent challenge in autonomous navigation remains the development of a reliable place recognition system. This paper presents an LiDAR-based place recognition solution, where a 3D point cloud is used to determine if two scenes correspond to the same location. To achieve this, a 3D descriptor is extracted from a limited area around the LiDAR head and from a broader area representing the entire scene. Two descriptors are compared using an attention-based deep learning network, with the output indicating the level of correspondence. Testing the proposed system on real-world data from various sources shows it performs better than existing LiDAR-based approaches. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that our system's performance can be optimized for navigation applications by adjusting certain parameters.

Video transcoding, a crucial task for adaptive streaming, demands computationally powerful processing to convert video codecs. Due to the varying capabilities of cloud servers, predicting and scheduling cloud resources is essential to optimize video transcoding performance. This research involves evaluating the computational requirements of video transcoding using OpenStack open-source cloud technology and real hardware, as well as developing a predictive modeling framework for cloud scheduling. Three distinct cloud configurations were used to analyze the computational needs of video transcoding and their energy consumption. The findings were then utilized to create a predictive modeling framework, which was tested under realistic scenarios to determine its accuracy. This research's results can aid cloud providers in designing and managing cloud infrastructure to optimize video transcoding performance.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech generation poses difficulties in modeling ongoing speech based on unknown past information, unseen future targets, and limited contextual influences. To tackle these challenges, MaskedSpeech framing proposes a novel approach that addresses contextual, past, and future considerations. In this approach, speech production is enhanced by masking strategies, which can be learned and integrated into a multi-task framework. Experimental evaluations conducted on the VCSpeech dataset demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms basic speech generation models in terms of accuracy and fluency.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation linked to an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, which includes the instance where there are conflicts between the symmetries at their boundaries. We provide a theoretical framework that, although rigorous, requires a non-perturbative approach to achieve accurate results. Therefore, we are forced to rely on approximations, both numerical and analytical, to gain insight into core structures and how they relate to charges. Our study reveals that, despite differences in symmetry boundary relationships, Q-balls can still provide a stable framework, particularly in situations where the symmetries complement each other. However, conflicts between the symmetries at their boundaries significantly complicate the situation, leading to an unpredictable relationship between core sizes and charges. Our research also indicates that, in certain scenarios, core sizes can be correlated with specific theoretical parameters, such as the mass ratio of specific fields, rather than the charge itself.

In cyclic cosmology, we investigate a simple model where dark matter is represented by an analog of the holographic principle. This model treats the cosmos as a holistic system, with the volume of the universe containing $V$ spatial dimensions reflecting the surface area of a surrounding space with $V+1$ dimensions. We examine the behavior of matter in this universe by employing a variant of the Dirac field and perform a perturbative analysis to derive the dark matter sector's effective action. As a result, we find that a term resembling the cosmic term emerges, linked to the radius of the enclosing space. Furthermore, we show that the holographic dark matter density proportional to the surface area of the universe can be achieved by incorporating a cyclic cosmology configuration. Additionally, we derive the frequency ratio of bosonic and fermionic particle modes, which takes the form $\frac{\nu_b}{\nu_f} = \sqrt{\frac{m_f}{m_b}}$, where $m$ represents the respective particle masses.

Gnutzmann and Smilansky previously developed a formula for the bond scattering matrix of a graph using a Hermitian matrix, for which an alternative proof has been devised, employing a method related to the zeta function of a graph. Furthermore, the formula has been broadened to cover regular coverings of graphs, and a novel 'L-function' concept for graphs has been defined, yielding a determinant expression. This has a corresponding outcome where the extended Gnutzmann and Smilansky formula can be represented by the graph's 'L-functions'.

We derive new conclusions regarding the Galois invariance of certain non-commutative extensions of Q. Specifically, if S^op is a finitely generated subalgebra of \bar Ql, where S is a finite set of complex embeddings of Q, and K is a subfield of \bar Ql involving S, the following conditions being sufficient: 1) K contains Q(s^-1) for all s in S; 2) the Galois group A_A associated with A and A' satisfies A_* \subseteq A'_*, given A and A' representing the non-commutative algebras corresponding to S and their possible extensions; 2) the Galois group A_A associated with A and A' satisfies A_* \subseteq A'_*, given A and A' representing the non-commutative algebras corresponding to S and their possible extensions. Additionally, we provide conditions under which we can determine the compositum of all subfields of \bar Ql containing Q(s^-1) for all s in S, as well as establishing connections between our results and prior work by J. Veloso.

A semi-analytic calculation is performed to determine the Belle II sensitivity to extra, semi-transparent particles of mass $m_A$ that deviate from standard model behavior in $B$ decays, specifically focusing on $B	o K
u ar
u$ and $B	o X\gamma$. This analysis is the most comprehensive to date for these processes, and it reveals intriguing discrepancies between predicted rates and current observations in the $B	o K
u ar
u$ process, with a predicted Belle II sensitivity to an area of parameter space not yet explored, even with the dataset that will be collected by the end of 2019.

This study offers a set of contextualized language models that are trained to recognize altered language from original text. We discovered through extensive testing that these models excel when identifying short passages with obvious changes, but struggle with longer texts and more subtle modifications. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that multiple models tend to misinterpret certain types of modifications, especially those involving vocabulary shifts, while also being prone to classification biases that affect the overall accuracy. Additionally, we found that contextualized language models are particularly sensitive to changes in syntactic structure and perform best with shorter sentences. These findings provide valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of contextualized language models for identifying altered language.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the relationship between spin and the emission spectrum to estimate the spin of heavy quasars by examining the spectrum of electrons in their surroundings.  Using the Radiative Transfer Code for Spectral Synthesis, we analyze the spectrum of electrons in the vicinity of heavy quasars with mass values ranging from 10 million to 50 million times the mass of the Sun, and estimate the spin of these quasars as 0.86±0.01.  Via the process of superradiance, these quasars can emit low-mass ultra-light scalar, vector, or tensor bosons with mass values ranging from 10^-22 to 10^-12 eV, and radiation lifetimes of up to 100 years.  These bosons, with masses in the range of 10^-17 to 10^-13 eV, can also explain the observations of cosmic rays with energies exceeding the predicted cutoff of conventional sources.  Additionally, the creation of heavy quasars with mass values greater than 10 million times the mass of the Sun is required for these bosons to function as effective providers of cosmic energy.  The supply of ultra-light bosons by heavy quasars also offers a potential explanation for the findings of recent atomic hydrogen surveys indicating the presence of massive ultra

A distinctive feature of neural cells within the zebrafish retina is their interkinetic nuclear movement between the poles of the cell, which is driven by changes in cell shape prompted by oscillations between mitotic and quiescent states. Through analysis of 3D data at different stages, a pattern emerges as the nucleus travels between the cell poles, and is further confirmed by tracking individual nuclei in live zebrafish retinas. The nucleus moves steadily towards one cell pole during the mitotic phase, only to move towards the other pole during the quiescent phase. Its movement during these phases is controlled by the contraction of the cell's cylindrical region, which in turn is governed by the tension at its junction with the adherens junctions at the cell poles. Our research reveals that the nucleus's movement is influenced by the contraction of the cell's cylindrical region, but that this contraction is insufficient to account for its speed. As a result, we propose that the extra force needed to move the nucleus at the appropriate speed is provided by the force generated by the contraction of the adjacent extracellular matrix. Our analysis also reveals that the nucleus's movement is impacted by the contraction of the cell's cylindrical region, but that this contraction is insufficient to account for its speed. As a result, we propose that the extra force needed to move the nucleus at the appropriate speed is provided by the force generated by the contraction of the adjacent extracellular matrix. In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, a specific separation step is often required to restore images from noisy, blurred inputs. A certain code, which we call the separation code or S-code, is associated with each measurement pattern in compressive video capturing or each color filter in a camera's sensor. The purpose of this code is to facilitate a computational process that can extract images from incomplete data. Given that certain S-codes are already implemented in camera sensors, it is imperative to investigate whether using these existing codes, rather than optimized ones, hinders the image restoration process. This study assesses the effectiveness of conventional Cartesian patterns, which are standard in camera sensors, and finds them to be ideal for handling various filter patterns. Moreover, we find that other patterns require specific properties, such as redundancy reduction or efficient transmission of low-frequency information, which can be met by structured or near-structured codes. Ultimately, this study demonstrates how to modify existing sensor codes to recover compressed video data efficiently.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active liquids in scenarios where there's a randomly distributed incompressible defect network. This defect network significantly slows down the particles' movement, especially in dimensions where space has more than two dimensions. In these dimensions, the particles can move quickly within the network's pockets, creating a liquid-like behavior that's unaffected by the defect network's details. However, in lower-dimensional spaces, the particles move so slowly that their dynamics are determined by a different rule and face the risk of paralysis. This rule can still provide insights that might be useful in designing active materials that can resist the slowing down effect of network defects.

Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as the primary means of communication. Due to their accessibility and private data storage, these emails are vulnerable to cyber threats and can serve as lucrative targets. Our proposed approach aims to examine research institutions' internal communication networks for potential security breaches. Initially, we gathered and analyzed email data from multiple research institutions, including three in Spain and one in Portugal. We applied an MIMIC-based method to identify vulnerable individuals within these networks. Subsequently, we updated the network dynamics by removing high-risk users and conducted comparative analyses of the modified network's structural characteristics. Our results indicated that removal of vulnerable individuals led to a significant reduction in network centralization and average degree, as well as changes in other key metrics. Due to the limited scope of our current data, we believe that our findings would be further enhanced by incorporating a broader range of research institutions.

Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new class of materials with a unique property: they exhibit exceptional van Hove singularities at the Fermi level. This phenomenon arises where Fermi surfaces intersect with areas of high energy density, creating highly exceptional van Hove singularities. We suggest that the pseudogap in these materials can be reduced by filling the van Hove singularities with electrons, and that the associated Fermi surface is stable against perturbations that break symmetry. Additionally, we predict that these materials can exhibit non-Fermi liquid behavior in the absence of a pseudogap.

Located in Aberdeen, Scotland, is a unique scientific testing facility called the Aberdeen Tunnel laboratory. This site is ideally suited for conducting experiments that involve studying spallation neutrons produced by cosmic rays interacting with the Earth's atmosphere. The laboratory is situated in a seismically stable tunnel deep within Aberdeen's bedrock, at a depth of approximately 90 meters where the atmospheric background noise is significantly reduced to -28.7 nanovolts per root square hertz. This low noise level, combined with the extensive spallation neutron flux at this site, makes it an excellent location for conducting sensitive experiments that involve detecting these neutrons and searching for rare decay processes of neutrinos.

Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity measurements to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  In addition to OCR, Natural Language Processing, a branch of Computer Science that enables computers to analyze and make sense of human language, can be used to verify the authenticity of Indonesian ID cards or KTP by analyzing the text derived from the OCR process.  This involves checking for valid identity number, date of birth, religion, marital status, height, weight, blood type, and nationality on the ID card.  If the extracted data meets these criteria, the ID card is deemed genuine.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation methods. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by causing their rotations to change over time. As a result, asteroids with short rotation periods may eventually reach a state of synchronization with their surrounding environment, leading to a stable rotation period. In a study involving three asteroids, (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos, their YORP values were calculated and found to be positive, indicating that the YO effect would increase their rotation velocities. It is also possible that these asteroids could eventually enter a state of synchronization with their surroundings due to the YO effect. In addition, the YO effect could be responsible for the rotation characteristics of (1620) Geographos, which shows signs of being in a state of synchronization.

The rise of social networks has altered the conventional understanding of public opinion formation. Our research examines online discussions on Instagram in response to political posts, with a focus on their evolution over time. We utilized a graph-theoretic approach, incorporating dynamic network analysis, to study discussions that developed around political influencers on Instagram. Our results reveal that users' contributions conform to a power-law distribution, both in terms of quantity and quota. We found that a small group of active users dominates the discussion, with a few leading the way. Our data shows that the information architecture of Instagram promotes an effect we call the "inflation of early adopters," where users who join the discussion quickly have a greater influence on its course. Our research also found that the attention of late joiners is drawn to posts with a large number of likes, creating a network phenomenon we call "equilibrium through variation." Our study provides insights for individuals with significant online presence, influencers, politicians, and businesses, highlighting the importance of engaging with their audience over time and taking into consideration the information environment of social networks.

We show that any collection of surface homeomorphisms that is bound in the Röllnik metric does not have compact subcollections. This result extends to collections of surface homeomorphisms that are bound in various other metrics, including the Chabauty metric. This type of non-compactness is consistent with findings in other areas of topology and dynamics. For example, bounded sets of surface diffeomorphisms do not have compact subcollections. Additionally, one-dimensional dynamics features compact subcollections of homeomorphisms with positive Lebesgue measure, which are not Röllnik precompact. Isomorphic mappings play a key role in our proof, with further implications including Röllnik precompactness of groups of surface homeomorphisms that contain a compact subcollection and have identity as their only common fixed point.

Determining stellar parameters for local, faint M-dwarfs is crucial for numerous applications, including the accurate assessment of planetary sizes and the discovery of newly formed planets in these stars. Conventional methods for measuring stellar parameters typically fail for M-dwarfs due to their limited number of spectral lines in the visual spectrum, which often results in poorly defined solutions and subsequently large uncertainties. In our research, we utilize a novel approach that analyzes UV spectral lines to measure the stellar parameters for M-dwarfs. Although the M-dwarfs selected for our sample are optically similar, our analysis reveals significant differences, with an average discrepancy of at least 50 K in temperature, 0.5 in surface gravity, and 0.5 in metallicity when compared to the field standards. Our study offers a comprehensive data set of stellar parameters for M-dwarfs, which is essential for interpreting the findings from upcoming missions such as TESS and PLATO, and our approach can be applied to a wider range of stellar objects over the next decade when high-resolution UV spectra become more readily available.

We propose a novel approach to achieving line ripples at an ultra-wide angle using dual metasurfaces in the optical range. By combining a negative phase shift from a chirped patch array and a positive phase shift from a corresponding notch array, we demonstrate the production of line ripples at 650 nm, 1.55 $\mu$m, and 2.1 $\mu$m wavelengths, including an approximately 60-degree angle. This technique can provide a means to increase line ripple generation efficiency and reduce its size, making it suitable for use in dual-dynamic metasurfaces. Numerical modeling utilizing Finite Element Methods verifies our design.

Although the theory of query evaluation has a long history, our current understanding of its fundamentals is still limited, as evident from recent studies indicating that numerous essential problems remain solved only by generalized and optimized approaches. In this research, we focus on a critical problem - solving general 1-N query circuits - and develop novel, generalizing insights through the use of self-joins. By leveraging self-joins, we are able to generalize previous results on 1-N query circuits with binary joins and derive new results for different types of joins. Our results demonstrate that certain 1-N query circuits with self-joins can be solved using only a small number of joins, whereas others require an arbitrarily large number of joins in the best case scenario. Furthermore, our findings involve the development of a specific 1-N query circuit that requires an exponentially increasing number of joins in order to solve it, indicating that the difficulty of solving 1-N query circuits increases exponentially with the number of conjunctive queries, in a scenario where self-joins are possible. This research also implies that an optimal solution to solving general 1-N query circuits with self-joins involves a different approach than that which is optimal for circuits with binary joins.

Multiple approaches to automating the creation of infinite word generators are discussed, building upon established techniques such as Rabin's signature and star-free languages, as well as more recent methods like weak semi-automata and counter-dependent automata. The unique characteristics and challenges of each approach are highlighted, along with the theoretical benefits that could be achieved through automation. A potential unified framework, combining elements of weak semi-automata and counter-dependent automata, is also proposed and discussed.

The investigation of neutral two-body decays of $B$ mesons offers valuable insights into their transition from a heavy quark to lighter quarks, primarily mediated by electroweak interactions. To explore these decays in depth, our research focuses on analyzing $B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ and $B^0_s \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays, specifically on measuring the momenta spectrum of the final state particles and determining the branching fraction of the $B \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decay for the first time. These quantifications contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of these transitions and their underlying physics.

A recent breakthrough has led to the successful observation of multiple coexisting attractors in a complex system that was previously examined through theoretical means. By utilizing harmonic forcing and a side-cavity mirror with reduced reflectivity, researchers uncovered a specific configuration that enables the discovery of previously unseen coexisting attractors in optomechanical systems. This finding has significant implications for its potential applications, such as triggering abrupt transitions between competing phases of polarization, and it has been validated through a variety of techniques, including measurements of forced response, Lyapunov exponents, and spectral analysis.

When working with skewed data, a suitable measure of variability is the mean absolute deviation from the median. However, traditional methods for estimating MAD are biased, overestimating the value. We introduce a new bias-corrected estimator for MAD, tailored for data following the alpha-stable distribution. By correcting the bias, our estimator provides a precise comparison of MAD values, even across differently sized data sets. We evaluate the performance of this estimator in realistic scenarios and find it exceeds the effectiveness of existing methods.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) visualizers like LIT, which produces simple 2D functions to approximate neural network behaviors, have been very successful so far. However, the ability of these methods to visualize multiple functions at once has not been explored yet. This has clear implications - if a method can only visualize one function at a time, it's likely a result of the method's limitation rather than a feature of the neural network. In a significant breakthrough, our research reveals that neural networks trained on diverse datasets possess a different property, which we call the'multiple function challenge'. To tackle this challenge, we introduced an innovative method called MPACT, which uses a unique activation function designed to generalize well. The activation function is made up of several parts, each responsible for discovering distinct patterns in groups, like shapes and colors. To test the limits of MPACT, we used it to visualize the behavior of multiple functions at once, especially in situations involving different coordinates and scales. In a surprising turn, MPACT performed even better when these conditions were harder to meet. Finally, we found that the patterns learned by MPACT are not only visually appealing but also easy to understand, which is evident from the fact that most of the learned examples can be described in just a few words.

Animacy, the quality of life associated with animals, has been observed to be reflected in how humans perceive and organize living beings from different species. Recent research suggests the ventral temporal cortex plays a key role in this animacy hierarchy, with studies using visual field perception tests revealing the complex structure of the hierarchy through patterns of damaged visual fields. These damaged visual fields can be broken down into basic features that combine to form more complex patterns, mirroring the hierarchy of living beings ranked by animacy. Our study builds upon this finding by mapping the structure of the animacy hierarchy in the ventral temporal cortex using data from perception tests with both monomorphic (cat versus dog) and polymorphic (mammal versus bird) stimuli. Our analysis of these patterns seeks to identify the underlying cortical organization that gives rise to these perceptions, with potential connections to the complex concepts of emergence and the complexity of cognitive systems.

The study proves the quantum unique ergodicity (QUE) for Hecke-Maass newforms at a convenient scale, specifically showing that almost all coefficients from these forms exhibit an expected distribution in alignment with the central lattice point perspective, particularly in cases involving real zeros or Landau-Siegel zeros. The proof builds upon previous work by Brumley, Brumley-Lawton, and Kowalski-Mertens, while also establishing relationships between QUE for Maass newforms and the distribution of zeros of L-functions. The findings also imply that Landau-Siegel zeros cannot exist.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to allow for the verification of quantum programs with reference to the behavior of other, potentially interactive, quantum programs. Our adaptation maintains the Hoare rules for preconditions and postconditions, while incorporating a judgment that relates to the expectation of a quantum program's outcome, subject to certain conditions. This has the advantage of expanding the range of properties that can be quantified in relation to a program's expectation, such as its overall energy or the probability of successful completion. We demonstrate the efficacy of this adaptation through several examples, including the successful validation of a program for simulating the LHG model, as well as a program for generating a uniform distribution. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of expected values for relational Hoare logic, enabling the quantification of an operator's expectation for a quantum program.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This study investigates how epidemics are affected by these events, using a susceptible--infected--removed model that includes a set of interconnected groupings, as the number of individuals in each grouping multiplies and the infections spread quickly within each grouping. By solving the model mathematically, researchers derived an approximate solution that reveals how epidemic progression is controlled by several factors, including the average number of individuals infected per infected person, the number of new infections generated by a super-spreader event, and the mobility between different groupings. These interactions can result in chaotic patterns of transmission, as seen in cases like the 2003 SARS outbreak in Hong Kong, where extrinsic factors like the availability of hospital beds contribute to escalating transmission.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with a cyclic collection of operators, labeled as T, operating on X. This paper explores the spectral properties of the operators within this cyclic collection. Initially, it establishes a link between the spectral type of a single operator and the spectral type of the entire cyclic collection. Subsequently, the paper identifies the discrete and absolutely continuous parts of the spectral type of the cyclic collection, incorporating criteria related to the compactness of certain operator functions. This research was previously presented in brief form at the 21st International Conference on Operator Theory.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to measure the radii of 304 young stellar clusters in 31 nearby galaxies using high-resolution Hubble Space Telescope images from the LEGUS survey. The custom analysis covered a wide spectral range, from ultraviolet to near-infrared. The measured radii were compared to previous estimates made by cluster makers, and a new statistical approach was used to determine the most reliable results while accounting for uncertainty. The findings revealed a broad distribution of cluster radii, with a notable peak at approximately 2 pc. Notably, the proportion of extended clusters increases with the age of the cluster. This trend is thought to reflect the structural changes within gas-rich galaxy regions as they evolve. The study also explored relationships between cluster radius, mass, and surface density, with results indicating that more massive clusters tend to have greater radii, likely the result of density variations within gas-rich galaxy environments.

We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states.

A sign-flipping problem exists in stochastic neural network methods, such as the neural network solution to the Hubard model, that arises when a minimization step falls outside a feasible region due to the constraint that network weights remain complex-valued. This problem can occur even with an extremely small learning rate. It has been discovered that applying a specific rotation to the mini-batch optimization method eliminates the sign-flipping problem, enabling the neural network to solve the Hubard model without initializing the weights in a specific 'phase'. This technique can be seen as a 'fourth way' of avoiding the sign-flipping problem in addition to initializing all weights to zero, applying constraints to the module parameters, or using the data-driven method. It has also been found that this technique can be employed to neural network models beyond the Hubard model.

Prime factorization plays a fundamental role in understanding the properties of integers. While every integer has a unique factorization based on specific prime numbers, the distribution of prime factors themselves follows a distinct pattern. As integers increase, the number of prime factors grows in accordance with the Dickman function $\rho$, which reflects this underlying trend. However, the relationship between $\rho$ and prime factorization is only apparent when considering large integers. The first few values of $\rho$ for specific scores (the sum of the number of prime factors of each integer in a range) reveal a cyclical pattern, which can be interpreted through a recursive formula that applies to any positive integer $x$. The formula indicates that $\rho(x)$ represents the number of items among the first $x$ positive integers that are eligible to be included in a set with $s$ elements, where only including $s$ elements in a set is permissible. The distribution of prime factors across all positive integers can be viewed as a series of overlapping intervals, each representing the possible range of values for $\rho$. The ratio of the length of the $s$th interval to the previous interval is consistently observed to be approximately 0.4, indicating that in a given interval, values of $\rho$ typically increase by one for every four consecutive increases. This relationship varies depending on the specific value of $s$.

Given any non-trivial free group basis change $\phi$, there exists a bijective mapping $\beta$ that translates words in $F_a$ to words in $F_b$, and a monoid homomorphism $\psi$ derived from $\phi$. For any free group basis change $\phi$, there exists a monoid homomorphism $\psi$ that induces homomorphisms $\alpha$ and $\beta$ on the associated monoid complexes, resulting in increased complexity rates and, under specific conditions, a relationship between the pre and post-image complexity rates.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to give machines similar abilities by enabling them to generalize between tasks without explicit direction.
We develop a novel method that allows unsupervised cross-task generalization in tasks with labeled data and where the input features remain the same.
By employing this approach, machines can learn to perform new tasks based on existing skills and adapt them to fit the requirements of the new task.
We particularly focus on boosting existing tasks using recently acquired skills in tasks where the task names are available for reference.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on multiple datasets and prove that it offers more than just a basic combination of the two methods by conducting extensive experiments.
In particular, we find that it effectively distributes learning between old skills and new information, achieves better performance by effectively utilizing relevant information, and simplifies model training by reducing unnecessary complexity.
We also explore possible ways to expand on this approach by considering more general cases and broader applications for cross-task generalization.
Overall, our method offers a groundbreaking solution for cross-task generalization and paves the way for further research on both theoretical and practical aspects of generalization.

This research introduces the m-ar-K-Fast Algorithm for Component Analysis, an novel method developed to identify latent components in a data set, based on the non-iterative ar-K-Fast Algorithm. Like its predecessor, the new method employs matrix transformations to estimate component scores and loadings, resulting in a direct and efficient approach. In addition, the proposed algorithm facilitates the specification of maximum degree of cross-covariance between latent variables, making it more versatile than the ar-K-Fast Algorithm. The proposed algorithm is tested on several real-world data sets, demonstrating its effectiveness and accuracy in identifying latent components.

This work offers an overview of requirements engineering in the gaming sector.
Existing research studies on this topic have been thoroughly examined.
Key characteristics of the gaming industry were identified and their connections to broader market dynamics discussed.
In addition, several potential areas for further research within this field were highlighted.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that settle the trade-off between privacy and performance, without relying on benchmark datasets, is therefore a significant challenge. The framework we introduced in this paper applies the theoretical analysis of private machine learning to develop a method for hyperparameter optimization. This optimization algorithm effectively balances the impacts of noise and randomization on private learning, and can be efficiently run on high-dimensional datasets. Our experiments show that this approach achieves superior performance in comparing private models relative to non-private baselines, and our findings on the theoretical and empirical aspects of private hyperparameter optimization raise novel research questions.

In this study, we establish a comprehensive framework for analyzing the underlying properties of a group G by drawing from a broad range of mathematical concepts, including the principles of compatibility, symmetry, and integration. At the heart of this framework is an abstract representation of a group's boolean structure, which is essentially a specialized version of the original structure. We demonstrate that this representation is a natural extension of famous morphosymmetric structures such as distributive laws, Frobenius laws, and closure laws. Furthermore, we explore various specific instances of this framework's applications to various aspects of a group, such as its automorphism system, permutation subgroup, and order, providing a unified perspective on them in the process.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly influence future cosmological research with its Visible and Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer instruments. The authors of this study analyzed how variable readout noise affects Gaussian processes used for noise modeling, as the instruments experience thermal fluctuations that cause 1 f noise. The model includes the impact of this noise on satellite photometry, particularly for the NISP instruments, which are designed to study galactic populations, the formation of galaxies, and the properties of dark matter. The authors demonstrate that modeling this noise is essential, particularly because it has a greater effect than other noise sources, and they recommend that individual readout channels be processed separately to account for differences in noise levels.

We performed an analytical study to examine the composition of the Milky Way disk using data from the APOGEE-2. The analysis was based on a two-component model consisting of an exponential and a ring-like structure. We evaluated the accuracy of the model by comparing it to three different datasets: APOGEE-GAIA, which used stellar velocities and compositions, and two mock datasets created through computational simulations. The results showed that the model accurately represented the composition of the disk using APOGEE-GAIA, with a high correlation coefficient of 0.96 for a comparison of the model's predicted compositions to the actual compositions. A further analysis involved using the model to identify and remove stellar populations that didn't fit the expected distribution, and then comparing the composition of the modified model to the composition of the original APOGEE-GAIA dataset. The findings showed that the modified model took into account most of the actual composition differences, with an exponential decay scale length of approximately 2.6 kiloparsecs and a ring-like structure radius of around 7.5 kiloparsecs. Additionally, the analysis revealed small composition variations within the disk, specifically a gradient of metallicity, carbon, and nitrogen in the exponential decay region, and slight abnormalities in the ratio of oxygen to iron in the ring-like structure.

Online rumors pose a threat to public order and need accurate information about their spread and influence. This paper proposes a new approach to tracking the dissemination of rumors by incorporating validation into the diffusion process. The approach is tested during the COVID-19 pandemic in China, as rumors spread rapidly through social media. The proposed method is compared to existing approaches by analyzing rumor diffusion networks in China during the pandemic. The results show that the proposed method surpasses existing methods in terms of similarity measures, such as precision, recall, and F1 score. Furthermore, the study finds that the influence of rumors can be measured by combining propagation speed and network reachability. The research provides a theoretical basis for evaluating rumor propagation and suggests future directions for studying rumor propagation and influence.

A novel catalog of 1200 planetary nebulae has been created for the Fornax cluster, constructed from H-alpha observations taken as part of the Fornax3D spectroscopic survey. These planetary nebulae were identified and extracted using an advanced algorithm, and spatially resolved H-alpha spectra were obtained for each one. A new approach was developed to estimate the distance to 31 Fornax cluster galaxies, yielding an average distance of 19.86 megaparsecs with a standard deviation of 1.85 megaparsecs. This method was cross-checked with standard planetary nebula density profiles, resulting in similar distance estimates. Additionally, the catalog shows that planetary nebula density profiles are consistent across the Fornax cluster, and significant variations in density were detected within the galaxies' central regions.

This paper introduces LifeStream, a flow processing engine designed to efficiently handle periodic streams on a large scale. LifeStream is a robust and high-performance platform capable of supporting complex event processing applications with both temporal and non-temporal queries. To optimize performance, LifeStream utilizes a combination of techniques such as time-space mapping, dynamic plan adjustment, and batch processing. Through comprehensive testing, LifeStream demonstrates its capability to support large-scale datasets and support over 1000 machines with periodic streams. Furthermore, LifeStream outperforms other flow processing engines and traditional databases, achieving up to 10 times faster results.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not require a metric to determine their properties. A specific property, called the bi-associate curve, was found to be a curve's own image when passed through a particular point. This property can be applied to a type of curve called the Bertrand curve, which has unique properties when it lacks a metric. The research extends the properties of these curves to include timelike curves, which are essential in understanding complex geometric situations.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

A new boundary feedback controller is designed to stabilize the Navier-Stokes equations in a rectangular domain with a slanted boundary. Unlike the Neumann boundary feedback controller, which relies on the derivative of the velocity along the boundary, this controller's stability requirements are more flexible and only need the velocity itself. Similar to the Neumann controller, however, the slanted boundary must be oriented at a right angle to the outer walls in order for the controller to function properly. A key aspect of this research involves developing a new Lie operator and derivative approach, which provides a generalized framework for boundary feedback stabilization in complex domains.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model divides the material into two separate components - a solid polymer phase and a molten phase - and incorporates the influences of temperature and crystallinity changes on polymer viscosity and heat transfer. Utilizing a finite element method simulation, the model predicts the development of crystallinity, temperature changes, and resulting mechanical deformations during various tests, including tensile and cooling tests, showcasing a close alignment with experimental evidence.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped FeSe through nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic properties using the full Ginzburg-Landau free energy for multi-orbital systems. The calculated magnetic susceptibility shows an exact singularity at the on-set temperature of superconductivity, following a $T$-linear behavior. Notably, the magnetic response breaks the orbital symmetry, charaterized by the parameter $\gamma$ which can be adjusted through strain or electron doping. Additionally, a $d$-wave symmetry of the superconducting order parameter is demonstrated, as well as a distinct relation between the Pauli paramagnetic effect and the symmetry breaking, where the absolute value of $\gamma$ can be estimated. These findings provide a sound theoretical basis for experimental design and interpretation in search of the Pauli paramagnetic effect in nematic superconductors.

The effectiveness of learning-based robotics systems significantly depends on the quality of their supervision. Since obtaining perfect ground truth from sensors is impossible due to their noisy nature, feedback rectification is inevitable. Current algorithms are designed with specific feedback types in mind, necessitating significant reworking in the presence of different feedback. In contrast, feedback-rectified supervision poses a more general supervision scheme that encompasses various forms of feedback. In this paper, we propose a novel paradigm that enables learning from a wide range of feedback types, which we refer to as PRS-learning (short for Partial and Rectified Supervision-learning). The proposed algorithm can efficiently learn from various forms of feedback, including those that are incomplete, incorrectly labeled, and generated by transforming true labels. We demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm over traditional methods by conducting comprehensive experiments under various noisy supervision settings, including inference in dynamic environments. Furthermore, we discuss the benefits of adopting a unified PRS-learning approach in the presence of feedback rectification.

Continuous phase modulation (CPM) detection techniques provide coherent and non-coherent performance close to optimal solutions, making them suitable for various applications and scenarios. This paper investigates the water-fading channel and evaluates the performance of conventional differential CPM detection with non-coherent phase estimation. We derive an approximate expression for the error probability in high signal-to-noise ratios and compare it to existing techniques. Furthermore, we analyze the modification of CPM symbols and demonstrate the trade-off between bandwidth efficiency and high-SNR error probability behavior. This research provides a modified differential CPM scheme that surpasses the conventional technique's delay performance.

The interaction between a neutron star and a black hole has significantly more complex dynamics than a neutron star-neutron star merger.  Due to the presence of asymmetries, shocks, and other phenomena, the gravitational wave signal emitted by these interactions may be influenced, which could impact their detectability by LIGO via gravitational wave analysis.  In addition, the likelihood of detecting a counterpart in other waves, such as X-rays or optical light, depends on the behavior of the neutron star as it collapses, which could result in a sudden cessation of gravitational wave data.  Taking into account the dynamics of core collapse, we determine the probability of observing a binary black hole/neutron star merger by considering all possible mergers of neutron stars and binary black holes within the mass range of $1.1M_{\odot}$ to $1.5M_{\odot}$.  We find that approximately $7.6\%$ of all possible mergers of this type are characterized by a sudden cessation of gravitational wave data following the collision of the neutron star with the black hole, and that the probability of observing such an event is as low as $0.17\%$.  This reduces to $0.13\%$ if we only consider collisions that result in the formation of a black hole of at least $2.5M_{\odot}$.  This implies that the overall rate of observable binary black hole/neutron star mergers remains extremely low, at $

A previous study investigated the quantum capacity and vacuum compressibility of spacetime using a general class of thermal sources. This study extends that work to all possible source configurations described by the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation, resulting in the determination of the logarithmic derivative of the reduced Wightman function. This derivative corresponds to the compressibility of vacuum states and, in certain source configurations, leads to the evaluation of the quantum capacity. Notably, for source configurations corresponding to the SU(2) Lie algebra, this Compressibility Quantifier yields the quantum capacity in the scalar quantum electrodynamics (QED) and Bose-Einstein condensate models.

Current deep learning techniques used in removing rain from images have achieved notable success. Nonetheless, they operate in an image-to-image translation framework which is bidirectional, meaning they require a pre-defined rain map as an input. Nevertheless, extracting accurate rain maps from output rain-free images remains a challenge. Moreover, feeding real rain maps to these models doesn't take into account that rain appears differently under varying lighting conditions. In our proposed framework, we mitigate these issues by incorporating the creation of real rain maps in conjunction with rain removal. We develop a method that learns to synthesize actual rain maps and integrate them with the removal model via image-to-image translation. Furthermore, we introduce a bidirectional model that learns to disentangle light-dependent appearances in real rain images and in removed rain images. This framework enables the synthesis of high-quality real rain maps that are compatible with the recovered rain-free images, and also enables the removal of real rain images. We validate our approach through a series of experiments showing that our model outperforms the competition in both rain removal and rain map extraction.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

The continuum problem represents a continuing challenge in modeling paired particles, as it arises when attempting to scale up a model of two particles to represent multiple particles continuing in a straight line. The issue becomes more pronounced when considering the motion of gases, plasma, and fluid gases. In this paper, a two-body theory is expanded upon, demonstrating how it addresses the continuum problem through accurate representation of particles in motion. Central to this approach is a modified kinetic theory that derives the pressure and heat transfer characteristics desired in a multi-particle scenario. The paper shows that pressure and heat transfer can be accurately represented by means of a specific four-dimensional integral, and further demonstrates the applicability of this approach to diverse multi-particle scenarios.
This study establishes conditions and proof of existence for a modified Branson-Paneitz equation under Navier boundary conditions on a finite region of n-dimensional Euclidean space.

Evaluating risk of drug consumption poses difficulties, and there is a need for effective, efficient tools. Our study utilized the Five Factor Model of personality to gauge the effect of conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, openness to experience, and neuroticism on drug consumption risk.
