We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The analysis focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of the system - the bending effect - which influences how the system's performance varies with different observations of the system's behavior. The study's main achievement is to develop an accurate method for measuring the bending effect and to show that it has a direct impact on the system's overall performance. The analysis also reveals how the bending effect is affected by two key factors: the nature of the system's underlying structure and the distance between the system's different components. The findings are then applied to a practical scenario involving the prediction of wind speeds.

This research targets addressing the security concerns associated with nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA). We introduce an encoding method that ensures a malicious user cannot decipher the intended recipient's information and, in addition, conveys a hidden message to a designated user. The encoding technique involves manipulating the power difference between the signals directed at different users, with the aim of generating a hidden subspace inaccessible to the eavesdropper. Furthermore, we develop an accurate estimation method for determining the signal-to-noise ratio of the eavesdropper's receiver, which, in turn, enables precise adjustment of the encoding technique to prevent unauthorized access. We evaluate the performance of the proposed scheme, indicating that it yields significant improvements in receiving the intended message at the designated user and preventing unauthorized access, with only a minimal loss in signal-to-noise ratio estimation accuracy.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an efficient, linearly convergent algorithm using a unique, two-step approach within a restricted domain. By leveraging a direct formula for the optimal rotation, the proposed method achieves significant computational efficiency. Moreover, by applying a technique called parallel block coordinate descent, the algorithm finds a solution within the restricted domain, making it feasible for large-scale problems. The study also provides conditions for a locally linearly convergent solution and demonstrates the algorithm's performance through numerical experiments on real-world datasets.

Emotion-related question annotation is essential for developing effective sentiment-based question answering models, but the process is labor-intensive due to the complex nature of human emotions. BERT-based systems have shown great potential in predicting potential questions, but their ability to handle emotion-related cues needs further exploration. This study focuses on enhancing the efficacy of BERT-based question annotation by identifying relevant cues and developing a method to integrate these cues into the annotation process. A pre-trained BERT-based model was utilized to predict likely question annotations in conjunction with the underlying text, leading to an increased percentage of accurate annotations from 43.05% to 56.95% in an Emotion-Based Question Annotation Dataset. This study's findings may serve as a foundation for future research on emotion-related question annotation, and the dataset developed is available for download at https://github.com/hjdwjdwj/ebqad.

This paper builds upon the concept of strategic contagion introduced in 'Energy, Contagion and Strategy: Modelling Individual Behaviour in Social Networks' by supplying a more comprehensive model that incorporates multiple round interactions between independent actors in a large network, who make decisions based on a range of objectives including maximising their own individual reward, complying with social norms, or a combination of both. We establish a key finding that in a model where actors have the capability to offer incentives to others, there are infinitely many pure equilibrium strategies available, and we demonstrate a particular approach to classifying these strategies according to the strength of cooperation displayed by the actors through analyzing a simplified version of the model. Furthermore, we introduce an 'energy' metric that signifies the degree of cooperation present in a network, and we prove that this metric remains unchanged across all equilibrium strategies. In addition, we introduce the concept of 'energy-founding' actors within a network.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct fluid dynamics solvers, such as the Stokes and Navier-Stokes equations, and to demonstrate its compatibility with a variety of fluid-solving techniques. To achieve this, we will use a reduced dimension approach for both fluid and solid components in a fluid-solid interaction scenario. In the case of small distortions within an elastic structure, such as an airfoil within a flowing fluid, the approach results in significant computational time savings, showcasing the effectiveness of this method.

For autonomous mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings, having an understanding of their environment's layout and configuration is crucial. Currently available navigation systems typically rely on direct neighbor connections in graph representations, which can lead to stability issues and poor performance. In response to this challenge, a novel method of representing spatial layouts has been introduced with the HiTMap algorithm. HiTMap constructs a hierarchical graph structure by establishing connections at varying levels of abstraction, where local relationships are represented at the local level and overall spatial configurations at the global level. This framework demonstrates enhanced stability and efficiency in generating navigation paths compared to traditional methods. The effectiveness of HiTMap is demonstrated through simulation testing in dynamic scenarios and around obstacles, as well as with the integration of sensory inputs from lidar sensors. The developed system has been applied to a mobile robot capable of learning from its experiences and adapting to changes in its environment.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Aggressive Detection Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect aggressive tweets in five target languages (Arabic, Spanish, French, Portuguese, and Russian). For the English subset, we employed BERT-based models in addition to conventional feature extraction with support vector machines, while relying on machine translation and meta-learning for the other languages. Our BERT-based approach successfully ranked first among the competing teams for the English subset, whereas our simplified strategies yielded competitive results for the other languages despite being relatively uncomplicated.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

We investigate the emergence of a spin-polarized magnetothermal effect in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic layer, specifically a MoX$_2$ moir\'e superlattice combined with a EuSe ferromagnet. Our model reveals that this phenomenon is caused by the interaction between the moir\'e orbitals of MoX$_2$ and the ferromagnetic layer's surface state. When this coupling is strong enough, it induces a significant difference in the thermal expansion coefficients between the spin-up and spin-down states, leading to a distinct thermal magnetosensitivity in MoX$_2$. This result suggests that these materials could be used for sensitive spin detection and to implement a spin-dependent photon-magnetism effect.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, a quantum hydrodynamics model reveals that the unique characteristics of plasmons in narrow gaps, like reduced loss and increased speed, can be achieved without the need for specific spillover values.

Intuitionistic normalization for a dependent type theory is optimized for applications where the presence of a normalization function significantly enhances the system's proof capabilities. This normalization capability serves as a fundamental tool for developing programs and proofs through two key methods: proof term extraction from proofs and modalities to break down problems into more manageable subproblems. Our research utilizes the Calculus of Constructions, a dependent type theory that incorporates modalities, to demonstrate the efficacy of a normalization technique called 'robust normalization'. This approach normalizes constructs safely, while minimizing the influence of external factors that could compromise normalization. As a result, 'robust normalization' remains impartial, providing a balanced evaluation of dependent constructs including types, proofs, and programs. Our implementation of 'robust normalization' is part of the CoCinC compiler framework.

This lecture is designed for undergraduate students who have basic knowledge in physics and mathematics. It introduces the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, emphasizing its fundamental characteristics and properties. The model's unique features make it an ideal vehicle for exploring essential concepts in topological quantum theory. We guide students through a series of calculations to identify the model's energetic levels, create wavepackets to study polarization, and compute the system's periodic behavior in a finite and infinite context. Topological properties are examined through the calculation of the invariant index in both time-domain and frequency-domain analyses. We conclude by outlining the requirements for a quantum transition to occur in topological phenomena.

In statistics, where data varies significantly, the standard models often fail to capture the complexity of the data properly. This issue is particularly prominent in cases where the data comprises a mix of distinct populations. For example, analyzing genetic data from different species requires distinguishing between individual species' populations. To handle such situations effectively, statisticians use complex models that can model data as a mixture of different components. These models can be interpreted as representing the population structure of the data, and their parameters can be estimated through optimization of the model's performance on the data. However, the complexity of these models can also be expounded through their convex dual formulations, which provide insights into their population structures as convex combinations of the individual species' populations. This, in turn, links these statistical models to Choquet theory and stochastic geometry, which study the geometric properties of these population structures. Hence, looking at these population structures through a geometric perspective offers additional insights that can be utilized in handling certain statistical challenges.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for supergravity in AdS$_5$×S$^5$ using unitarity-based methods, specifically focusing on the grassmann component of the supergravity amplitude. By leveraging an established relationship between supergravity and certain QFTs, we expressed the adS amplitude as a sum of QFT amplitudes, relating the former's boundaries to those of the latter. This understanding helped explain the observed spurious boundary behaviors at large angles in previous studies. Moreover, our outcome confirms the previously proposed equations for Correlation Function Representation of adS amplitudes.

Recent efforts to accelerate high-level object-based languages with parallel processing capabilities on GPUs have been hampered by a lack of effective memory allocation techniques suitable for these devices. As a solution, we propose DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed for object-based programming on GPUs. This allocator utilizes a binary tree data structure and parallel insertion algorithms to efficiently allocate memory, reducing conflicts and waste. In experimental evaluations using C# programs and the.NET Core framework on Windows, DynaSOAr consistently outperformed other memory allocators in benchmark tests, achieving significant improvements of up to 6 times over the.NET Core allocator and 2 times over a specialized GPU memory allocator.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a paired Mn adatom, simulations revealed a split YSR state and distinguished between intrinsically paired YSR states by utilizing spin-polarized band structure calculations. Furthermore, analysis of a paired Mn adatom conducted with tight-binding band structure calculations replicated experimental findings, while examination of a nearest-neighbor Mn dimer on Nb(110) showed little agreement with experimental results, highlighting the need for further investigation.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural surfaces to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit neural network function, allowing it to adapt and learn boundary shapes across different classes. By exploiting the algebraic properties of the Fourier series, FourierMask reduces computational costs and model parameters by half, without losing precision. Our approach learns boundaries and shapes across the MS COCO dataset with real images, demonstrating superior performance and efficiency in instance segmentation through Fourier transformation.

This study examines how a bounded morphosis, defined as a composed map f:N->R^d within a N-dimensional manifold N, affects the structure of its image when projected onto a flat d-dimensional space. Specifically, it investigates the exterior range R of the morphosis, determined by the minimum distance from any point in N to the image of any retracted portion of N. The study demonstrates that if an area-minimizing morphosis within a bounded region of R^d has a finite R^k component and meets specific criteria, then the range R^{d-k} of the composed map is also finite. The study also extends this concept to thin layers in R^d and broad layers in R^k\times R^{d-k}.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds, which cover approximately 10% of Earth's surface and play a crucial role in global energy balance. Cloud tomography, an emerging field, offers promise in overcoming these limitations by providing detailed cross-sections of cloud morphology. Tomographic reconstruction from simultaneous observations of incoming satellite rays is a promising approach, which we have successfully demonstrated using data from the MISR and MODIS satellites. However, this process is complicated by the limited amount of information obtained by each satellite sensor and the inherent noise present in the data. We have developed a novel technique to recover the density of space-based cloud tomograms by directly applying the least-squares method to MISR and MODIS data before accounting for viewing angle effects. Which we have found to yield the most accurate results. Additionally, we have established standards for the quality of tomographic data produced by this technique, including a level of noise below 5 and a tomographic slice thickness below 300 meters. We have also successfully applied this technique to detect the "hidden core" of opaque convective clouds, which has significant implications for the study of cloud dynamics.

We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts ion acceleration via a self-induced transparency effect. Our investigation focused on a linear change in frequency, resulting from a superposition of two lasers. This specific setup leads to increased ion charging and enhancement of the self-induced transparency phenomenon through a process that relies on chirped pulse propagation. A particular phase relationship between the two lasers is necessary for this enhancement, and it produces a greater than tenfold increase in ion charge. Moreover, this arrangement facilitates the achievement of high field strengths, over 100 GV/m, despite the presence of plasma losses.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune candidates with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the planets' positions and applying the Van Hammershmidt rule, the team determined the most favorable planetary environment is that of the planet with the $9.531$ day period. Based on $TESS$ photometric temperature estimates and this planet's semi-major axis, the team calculated a surface temperature suitable for liquid water to exist. The team also analyzed galaxy evolution models, in addition to observing this system in the $z$-band with the $LAMOST$ spectrograph, in order to gather more information about its composition and whether it operates in the habitable zone.

We investigated the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a method that incorporates large supercells and relaxes both the guest and host atoms.  The results show that nitrogen has higher activation energies for diffusion than hydrogen, in line with experimental observations.  Conversely, carbon exhibits higher activation energies than hydrogen for both the cage and bulk phases.  Furthermore, our findings indicate that both carbon and nitrogen have higher binding energies to oxygen vacancies compared to hydrogen, justifying their nontoxic nature when doped into TiO2.  The results also demonstrate the need for large empty cages around carbon to minimize its energetic advantage over hydrogen, in contrast to nitrogen which consistently displays higher activation energies than hydrogen.  Our research suggests that both carbon and nitrogen defects can potentially improve TiO2's photostability when incorporated at low concentrations.

One potential method for detecting top quark production at the Large Hadron Collider involves identifying the unique signature of top quarks and anti-quarks being produced in a process called elastic production. However, this process has a very faint signal, often masked by more prominent events, making its detection extremely challenging. To overcome this difficulty, researchers are using sophisticated techniques such as machine learning to these effects and gain insight into the data. By analyzing data from the LHC, we have established limits on the production rate of certain processes involving top quarks and anti-quarks being produced elastically, alone or in combination with other particles, along with bounds on the total cross-section of these processes. These limits range from already quite precise to potentially breakable ground in future data sets.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics.  The properties of thermal plasma within these clusters are influenced by turbulent motions, gas movements due to gravitational forces, and other effects, albeit the absence of direct observational evidence for turbulence.  X-ray emission line studies have the potential to provide conclusive evidence for turbulence in the intra-cluster medium.  However, existing studies have been limited by the low signal-to-noise ratio of emission lines or the small size of observed regions.  A study of the [O III] line with high signal-to-noise ratio and obtained from the XMM-Newton and Chandra observations of the galaxy cluster Abell 2199 used a new approach to determine the line's shape.  By utilizing structure functions and multiple observations, it was possible to increase the signal-to-no-noise ratio further, thus leading to a better understanding of how the line's shape varies with distance.  However, a significant challenge in this study was addressing the issue of measurement ambiguities, specifically the problem of identifying the most reliable estimate for how the line's shape varies with spatial distance.  This problem is a significant obstacle in the study of turbulence in the intra-cluster medium using X-ray emission lines.  It must be resolved through a deeper statistical analysis or a significant improvement in the sensitivity of X-ray detectors.  Until then, the study of turbulence in the intra-cluster medium will rely heavily on theoretical models and numerical simulations of plasma dynamics

An upper bound for a graph property 'R' on Ramsey numbers can be described as how many copies of 'R' are needed within a single tone of an infinite complete graph, where it is understood that an upper limit exists. The term 'richness' is often interchangeably used with 'upper bound' in this context. The term 'ramsey upper richness' refers to the fewest number of instances of 'R' needed within a single tone of an infinite complete graph, where it is known that such an upper limit exists. The term 'ramsey upper richness' can be used for upper bound problems, setting a minimum count of a specific graph property 'R' within a single tone of an infinite complete graph. The problem of determining the ramsey upper richness of complete infinite graphs in two tones has been completely resolved in a 2019 paper by T. Krawcewicz and M. Lozano, who found the ramsey upper richness to be 4 for most 3-colored complete infinite graphs. This article expands on that finding, also successfully resolving the corresponding 4-colored problem.

Located within the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation of molecular material. Recent studies have suggested that the CMZ is home to a significant number of star-forming regions and is narrowing down as a result of gravitational forces. Previous research has proposed an anisotropic density framework to accurately model the distribution of molecular materials in the CMZ. To further test this theory, we analyzed the 86.4 GHz H2O maser sources in the CMZ and calculated their two-dimensional correlation function. Our data revealed a specific anisotropic configuration characterized by 300 degrees of opening angle and a radial correlation length of approximately 11.5 parsecs. This anisotropic pattern is similar to that of the Large Magellanic Cloud's (LMC's) star-forming regions and may indicate an inner "bar" structure within the LMC. However, we cannot rule out the possibility of this feature being an intrinsic property of the LMC. Our research provides a statistical basis for modeling the distribution of molecular materials in the CMZ and has implications for the formation of the CMZ's ring-like structure.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to detect Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called the Eye Closure Profile (ECP) to quantify the blinking pattern of each eye and developed a straightforward yet effective classification algorithm using these profiles. ECP profiles are extracted from video clips, analyzed in 1-second intervals, and then combined with contextual information about the video's timing and related medical data. These profiles are then employed to train and evaluate our detection method through a straightforward classification process. We have conducted exhaustive experiments in a simulated environment and with real-world video data, showcasing our approach's superiority over established methods and highlighting the importance of context in accurate diagnosis. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the feasibility of our method on limited data, emphasizing the need for enlarged and controlled datasets to further refine our detection method.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d by simulating their parity-based sector. This parity sector contains a two-dimensional Hilbert space that can be effectively utilized with qudits by separating the parity states. We found that using qudits leads to a decrease in classical noise error rates when simulating this parities sector. Specifically, we observed that for $s=2$, there's approximately a $s^2$ factor improvement in average error rate when comparing qudits to qubits. This improvement translates to longer simulation times or better control over the quantum processor. We also discovered that using qutrits instead of qubits allows for the incorporation of more stable higher-dimensional states, thereby prolonging the duration of usable simulations. Finally, we found that while noise in QED is primarily spatially uncorrelated, there's still a significant advantage to using qudits over qubits in this scenario.

Research indicates that positrons are emitted through the interaction of lasers with materials, specifically when taking a thin film covered with a semiconductor material and irradiating it with an ultra-high power laser. By examining the emission of positrons perpendicular to the film surface, our findings show that the density of emitted positrons can increase significantly, up to 10^18 per second, if the emission occurs in a quantum electrodynamics-dominated region. This happens because of the accumulation of charge on the surface of the semiconductor, which creates an intense electric field that directs the emission of positrons in a polarized state. This discovery of densely packed, polarized positrons may lead to further development in the field of particle physics, specifically in research involving precise measurements of light and particle interactions.

A group of order m by n (where m and n are positive integers or infinity) has polynomial width r if there are r generators that cover all subgroup sizes. We determine which finite groups have a polynomial width and categorize them based on the number of generators required. Specifically, a finite group with a polynomial width either has a width of 1 (meaning it's cyclic) or a width of infinity for some r, indicating it can't be generated by a finite number of subgroups with a wide base. Additionally, all groups that can be generated by a finite number of subgroups fall into abelian groups with a finite width.

This research develops a fully-integrated temperature sensing unit with a built-in temperature detector, which utilizes a single CMOS chip with a temperature range of 0.6V to 1.8V. The temperature detector employs a sub-threshold PMOS resistor with a high sensitivity of negative resistance variation in relation to temperature. In contrast to prior works, this design surpasses the limitations of sub-threshold operation by utilizing a bi-directional current mirror to overcome the inability to measure decreasing bias currents. The temperature detector features a minimal area of 20$\mu$m$\times$34$\mu$m and incorporates two digital conversion methods to calculate the temperature based on the detector's output. These methods result in accurate temperature readings with small standard deviations of 0.24$^\circ$C and 1.4$^\circ$C for models C and D respectively, along with conversion energies of 4.5nJ and 1.06nJ. The designed and fabricated chip features a 0.6V to 1.8V operating range, incorporating 48 temperature detectors with unique identities to facilitate distribution and calibration of temperature data. Experimental outcomes at room temperature yield precise temperature readings up to 70$^\circ$C.

Three-dimensional simulations of stars rely on the approximation of an axisymmetric magnetic field to also apply to their outer layers. This assumption is politically correct, meaning it holds stability, due to an underlying principle that any highly unstable magnetic field formations would be expelled by the star's matter transport processes. A recently discovered phenomenon, however, poses a question to this assumption, where a specific setup of a strong, unstable magnetic field within a star is shown not to be expelled by the transport processes, but instead remains stable for a significant duration. This stability is attributed to a slow-alignment effect of the magnetic field with the star's rotation, causing a stabilizing force through the generation of differential rotation within the star. This discovery implies that stars with high rotation rates and strong magnetic fields may experience slow-alignment interactions, influencing their internal dynamics and behavior.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve complex problems by translating them into an FRG framework, which involves a set of differential equations that represent the renormalization group flow. In this paper, a novel approach is introduced to address these differential equations using numerical fluid dynamics methods, which enables researchers to handle the complexities associated with the original problems. By employing this approach for zero-dimensional quantum field theories, such as the O(N) model, the introduction of a limited number of scalar fields transforms the renormalization group flow equations into a simple fluid dynamics scenario. This simplification allows the introduction of multiple exact initial conditions, which can be derived from field theory perspectives. These initial conditions, in turn, enable the precise numerical solution of the renormalization group flow equations in this simplified scenario. Various properties of the theory can be accurately determined by analyzing the solutions to the fluid dynamics equations at different renormalization group scales. This introduces a new level of precision in the study of quantum field theories. In addition to standard parameters such as the fixed-point location and flow equation scaling, this approach also makes it possible to analyze the speed at which the system equilibrates and the correlations within the system across both space and time dimensions. This study is relevant to ongoing investigations in the physics of quantum fields, particularly in areas like the properties of hadrons and the behavior of phase transitions.

Despite significant achievements in music processing through neural networks, several fundamental challenges remain unresolved. One key issue is the lack of a precise note-sequence representation, often addressed by utilizing existing databases of recorded music. Another significant hurdle is the limited understanding of music based on written scores alone. To accelerate music improvement through automated assessment, we have developed a comprehensive system called Pied Piper, which utilizes a cutting-edge neural network to generate comprehensive and precise annotations for both chord and melody in written music scores. This advanced model, incorporated into a Quest framework, effectively bridges the gap between traditional analysis methods and artificial intelligence by providing accurate results for a diverse range of scores and has been thoroughly validated through comprehensive testing and a user-friendly interface.

We establish a theoretical foundation for geometric frameworks on Lie groupoids and stacks, building on the work of Kapranov and Voevodsky. By showing that the functors in question are representable, we can then relate them to category theoretic concepts such as composites and coproducts. This allows us to define the notion of a geometric framework over a base stack, and prove that the associated hom-set yields a manifold when the base stack is a Lie groupoid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the functors from a stack to the manifold of maps from a Lie groupoid to a base stack are representative of the hom-sets of the latter, and that this relationship holds for stacks with source and target maps.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass-to-flux ratios, indicating enhanced gravitational pressure, and a wider distribution of mass-to-radius ratios compared to their starless counterparts.  The former characteristic persists even after removing outflows from the analysis, and it becomes the core's intrinsic property as it undergoes a transition from starless to protostellar stage during its evolution.  The finding is interpreted as evidence that increased gravitational pressure in cores contributes to the creation of molecular outflows, and it could serve as a milestone in the evolution of starless cores, marking their transition to protostellar stages.

Godel modal logics have proven useful in analyzing theories with diverse language capabilities, including arithmetical theories and their set-theoretic extensions. Godel modal logics are an extension of classical modal logics, incorporating Godel modal logics has the capability to tackle problems involving the consistency of theories. By leveraging relational structures and Boolean algebras with operator, this research provides a comprehensive explanation for satisfiability in Godel modal logics, including their extensions with Godel modal operators and their combination with classical modal operators. Specifically, this study identifies the essential conditions for satisfiability in these structures and algebras, enabling a straightforward derivation of existing results and a new approach to establishing the satisfiability of formulas in extension of Godel modal logics with sensitive Scarpino axioms.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data.

We're investigating a theoretical random field model on a sphere, specifically one that remains stationary over time. Our analysis focuses on an important aspect of these models – their initial conditions – and applies advanced mathematical techniques to derive a specific statistical measure. This measure, called the mean squared prediction error, is crucial for understanding how well future values of the random field can be predicted based on past observations. Our key finding is a innovative computational method that can calculate this prediction error quickly, requiring only a single step through future time points rather than an exhaustive consideration of all possible combinations of past and future values. This improvement is particularly significant for researchers studying the long-term behavior of random field models.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are taking a two-pronged approach, simultaneously pursuing the direct and indirect paths. The direct approach involves detecting UHECRs directly, while the indirect approach focuses on identifying the sources of UHECRs by locating the facilities or objects associated with extensive air showers generated by UHECRs using neutrino detectors such as IceCube. Here, we present the results of the largest search yet conducted for spatial correlations between neutrino detectors and UHECR facilities or objects, covering over 11,000 UHECR events with energies above 5 EeV and observed angles between 6 degrees and 6.44 degrees with respect to the direction of UHECR arrival. For the first time, we update the detection statistics for multiple high-energy sources, including supernova remnants, supernovae, long gamma-ray bursts, and binary neutron star mergers, as well as all neutrino sources detected by multi-peaked neutrino events and sources classified as such, and we also expand the inquiry to encompass all neutrino events above 0.1 PeV and observed angles between 4 degrees and 10 degrees with respect to UHECR arrival. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach using random walk theory to predict the density of neutrino detectors in regions associated with UHECR arrival directions

The flow of liquid foams is significantly influenced by two main factors: the arrangement of bubbles and the nature of the liquid surface. Despite this dual influence, researchers have focused mostly on the geometric structure of the bubbles when studying the flow. In contrast, this study reveals the crucial role that surface tension plays in the flow by transferring stress laterally across the liquid surface. The transferred stress is shown to be the same as the shear stress experienced by the bulk liquid, which is the result of the liquid's viscosity multiplied by the shear rate. However, this transferred stress has a critical limit, beyond which it disrupts the stability of the foam surface, leading to stick-slip behavior during flow. This phenomenon is seen in both thin and thick foams, although it occurs at vastly different shear rates due to the difference in liquid surface relaxation times.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

The motion of a fluid within a Hele-Shaw cell, when subjected to external influences, can exhibit varied patterns of growth, influenced by the presence of a rotating inner cylinder. By observing the behavior of an invasive species that disrupts the stability of the fluid, we have found that, when the cylinder rotates quickly, the pattern of growth changes to an asymmetrical one, affected by the curvature of the cell. This asymmetry allows the species to occupy a larger section of the cell. Additionally, the shape of the cell can be modified to increase the species' survival chances. The pattern of growth and the resulting asymmetry have been described mathematically, and the discovery suggests that the unique feature of such systems could be linked to the presence of fingering instabilities.

Building on a novel method introduced earlier, using Hamiltonian trajectories instead of molecular mechanics forces in MD simulations yields consistent results with experimental findings for the expansion phase of a model system with attractive and repulsive interactions. The method successfully addresses the challenge of maintaining a constant phase space volume during expansion, a requirement for thermodynamic equilibrium. The novel approach uses simplified potential energy functions that maintain the system's stability and allow for a set of stable Hamiltonian trajectories to be defined. The results show that using this method for the expansion phase of a model system leads to consistent outcomes with experimental data, regardless of the initial conditions. The proposed method may offer a way to achieve thermodynamic equilibrium in models with complex phase spaces.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of 3-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCCH) at twice the sensitivity is also reported, with a column density roughly five times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. The calculated abundances for CCH and CN radicals connected to the cyclopentadiene ring are relatively low, at around 0.005-0.007, which is significantly less abundant than the cyanoacetylene ring. The comparative analysis of CCH and CN abundances in the cyclopentadiene and benzene rings reveals that CCH is twice as abundant in the cyclopentadiene ring, whereas CN is twice as abundant in the benzene ring, thus providing insight into the formation mechanisms of these molecules. The ethynyl substitutions on the cyclopentadiene and benzene rings are believed to have no effect on the ring closure, which remains unlikely. Instead, ring closure is impeded by the presence of an internal hydrogen atom in 1- and 3-ethynyl-1,3-c

In neural machine translation, research focuses on improving translation quality by preventing loss of information when generating each word. This paper introduces a new approach called look-ahead focus, which aims to address this issue. This approach involves identifying relevant words and translating them at once by using a contextually rich context vector. We evaluated our method through various experiments and found it to be a viable solution to the problem. The code and model used in this study are available on GitHub.

The significant change in computing needs from simple client-server relationships to complex, distributed systems led to a need for a new paradigm - service-oriented architecture. This shift created opportunities for new technologies to emerge, and one such technology was grid computing. To understand the evolution of grid computing, researchers developed a theoretical framework based on translation that analyzed the development of this technology from both technical and social perspectives. Utilizing a case study of the open-source grid engine, Globus Ox, these findings were explored, and the results indicated that the translation of technology into practice involved more than just technical solutions but also social negotiations that shaped its development and implementation. Furthermore, the incorporation of human agency into the translation process revealed new insights into the development of grid computing, and this framework can be applied to study the adoption of other technologies.

A unified dark matter-model is presented which incorporates a dissimilar energy density component in addition to the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, comprising two parameters. The model's primary component is characterized by an exponential decay process where dark matter energy density is steadily depleted by a consistently increasing dark energy density. Furthermore, this model facilitates a constant rate of neutron proton conversion, resulting in a steadily increasing dark energy density at a rate equivalent to the conversion rate. A specific conversion rate is determined through successfully matching the model to the observed cosmic abundance of dark matter, whereas the constant decay rate is derived from the conversion rate. The model's parameters are examined through Monte Carlo simulations in the context of the Planck dataset, with a subsequent investigation of its cosmological implications. Additionally, the model is used to make predictions for the density parameters $\rho_m$, $\rho_r$, and the baryon dispersion metric $s$.

In small group learning environments, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creative confidence, effective communication, and a spirit of inquiry, ultimately leading to successful career outcomes. Unfortunately, many primary students lack curiosity, a trait that is essential for the effective implementation of project-based learning. To address this issue, we propose a novel theoretical framework that combines media process theory and distributed cognitive theory to better understand how individual curiosity levels are influenced by combined oral and written reflections on exciting learning experiences. Our subsequent design-based research involves the development of a curriculum that encourages curiosity through combined reflections on enjoyable learning activities and subsequent discussions of those reflections. We collected and analyzed video and audio recordings of 120 primary students as they went through this process, examining how individual curiosity levels changed over time and what verbal and non-verbal behaviors distinguished high-curiosity students from their low-curiosity counterparts. Our findings reveal specific behaviors associated with high curiosity, particular to project-based learning, and highlight the importance of controlling for prior interest when studying curiosity during learning activities.

This research introduces a novel Gaussian process model, centered on Mat\'ern principles, that can be applied to complex datasets represented as graphs. Unlike current Gaussian process models, which are often limited by their ability to scale efficiently to large datasets, this approach takes advantage of the graph structure to achieve both theoretical convergence guarantees and significant performance improvements in practice. We demonstrate that the proposed model achieves comparable or better accuracy compared to multiple state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmark datasets while significantly outperforming these methods in terms of running time.

Urban road detection through crowds of vehicles offers high yield but is hindered by low precision in initial detections, leading to poor classification performance. We have developed a comprehensive detection framework that systematically addresses these challenges with a hierarchical approach. Firstly, the framework filters out irrelevant detections through a road network-based validation process. Secondly, it eliminates ambiguities in the crowds by ranking vehicle detections based on their reliability. Thirdly, a classifier with a road network context is used to differentiate between urban roads and other areas. We have evaluated our framework with real-world data, achieving a significant increase in accuracy with a small number of vehicle rankings. Our code is publicly available for research purposes.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter on light neutrino and dark matter sector effective field theories. To understand these implications, we first analyze existing J/ψ decay data to determine the minimum number of electromagnetic photons required. Utilizing the established framework and including beyond-Standard Model fields, we compare the predicted photon spectra for various neutrino and dark matter models. For example, we find that form factor-induced sub-lattice corrections can lead to phonon production, as seen in J/ψ → γ + phonon. Furthermore, we demonstrate that neutrino and dark matter models can result in J/ψ → 2γ, 3γ, or 4γ decay, with the minimum being J/ψ → γ + photon. Additionally, we observe that the J/ψ → γ + photon process can contribute to hephron production in proton-proton collisions. Moreover, we find that the J/ψ → γ + photon process can be dominated by the contribution of a neutrino or dark matter field with a mass less than 10^4 TeV.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) method as a dimensional domain-independent variation of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). While traditional MSSA can be viewed as conducting multiple independent SSAs, this approach enables the exploration of multivariate functions across various dimensional spaces, such as bivariate time series and hyperbolic trajectories. Unlike conventional SSA, which focuses primarily on identifying pattern components, MFSSA reconstructs the original data using a combination of pattern and trend components, ensuring continuity. Developed within an R environment, the MFSSA package offers a versatile solution for analyzing multivariate data across various dimensional domains, offering a solution for the ongoing challenge of researching multivariate functional time series.

Deep learning-based automated emergency systems have been introduced to enhance road safety by identifying and notifying authorities to potential dangers, such as vehicles traveling through intersection obstacles. These automation technologies are now used in various intersections across Asia, specifically in China, India, and Southeast Asia. While they have been advertised as effective and efficient, the underlying algorithms remain secretive, hindering understanding of their performance. Recent research aimed to investigate the efficacy of these automated emergency braking systems in real-world scenarios. Initially, the investigators discovered the systems' ability to recognize critical situations and react promptly. However, further analysis revealed the systems' tendency to overreact to certain non-critical incidents and fail to respond adequately to more severe events. The research proposed two explanations for these findings: the systems' overdependence on single features and their lack of adaptability to changing environmental conditions. Based on these findings, the authors presented two potential defense strategies: the use of feature selection techniques and the implementation of adaptive methods. The study's results can be seen as preliminary steps, and it is hoped that they will spur interest in this emerging area and guide further research into the development of more effective automation technologies.

The global persistence of a random walk except for its starting point can be understood by examining its local time on specific levels. We establish an asymptotic formula for the sum of the one-dimensional random walk's local time spent at zero, divided by $t$ for $t$ equal to $n$ times some positive integer $n$. The expression is in terms of the derivative of a function related to the local time at zero and can be written as $\frac{1}{c}\left(\frac{L_0(t)}{t}\right)\to 2\frac{d}{ds}L_0(s)|_{s=t},$ where $c=2-\frac{2}{3\pi}\approx 1.567$. The result verifies a conjecture made by Yor and Burchell in 2014.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides the plasma necessary for these experiments, and it operates in two modes: an DC discharge mode and a helicon mode. This study focuses on the plasma characteristics of the source when it is operating in helicon mode. When the source is functioning in this mode, a fully ionized plasma with a uniform density is produced in a short time due to the high frequency of the helicon wave, which validates the design of the source.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced computer algorithms to assist with nucleus segmentation, which can be time-consuming and labor-intensive. However, conventional approaches typically focus on producing smooth boundaries at the expense of overall performance, resulting in subpar results when directly applied to microscope images containing noisy and varying cell sizes. To break this barrier, this research introduces a new method called W-Net, which is an advanced convolutional network that delivers exceptional nucleus segmentation results despite its straightforward design. By dividing the segmentation process into two distinct stages, W-Net ensures both precision and flexibility at each stage, allowing for more robust and adaptable nucleus segmentation. The team behind this research further validates its effectiveness by comparing W-Net to other leading nucleus segmentation models.

Let's consider a non-archimalian global field of characteristic not two and denote its absolute value by the symbol $.|$. For an integer $d$ greater than one, let's denote by $X_{d}$ the set of functions from the rational numbers to the set $\{0,1\}$, such that for any rational numbers $r$ and $s$, if $|r|_{{\mathbb{Q}}}|s^d=_{{\mathbb{Z}}}$1, then $X_d(r) = X_d(s)$. Our purpose here is to prove that the map $\psi \mapsto \psi\cdot \text{Nrd}^{-1}$, where Nrd denotes the reduced norm, establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the set of characters from the rational numbers to the group $SO_{2d-1}(\mathbb{Q}_s)$ or $Sp_{2d-1}(\mathbb{Q}_s)$ to the set $X_d$, for any non-Archimedean place $s$ of the field $\mathbb{Q}$.

A graph G is considered traceable if every vertex is visited exactly once during a Hamiltonian path. In this study, we investigate how the property of having a hamiltonian path is inherited when a graph is transformed into its repeated line graph. Our findings also reveal that this inheritance does not hold when the line graph is transformed, demonstrating this phenomenon for specific types of graphs, including cyclic graphs and graphs with a hamiltonian path index of two. Nevertheless, we are unable to make a general conclusion regarding graphs with a hamiltonian path index of three or higher.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory medications, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, necroptotic cell death. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the impact of external factors on the reward signal is established, and this is demonstrated through a practical application using data from a real-world reinforcement learning task.

A blockchain-based smart contract is a complex program with inherent risks, making it vital to thoroughly test and validate the code before deploying it. Refinement types offer a powerful tool for predicting a program's behavior and ensuring its safety. By linking refinement types to existing contract libraries, developers can accurately predict outcomes and prevent unexpected behaviors. Our project, HELMHOLTZ, is a refinement-type validator for Tezos smart contracts. It allows users to define safe behaviors for contracts using refined functions and validates the code against Michelson, Tezos' stack-based programming language. Due to Michelson's static type checking, validation is efficiently carried out as a type-checking operation. Our project is distinguished by its combination of high-level refinements and micro-validations, offering both general-purpose and contract-specific validation capabilities. By leveraging Michelson's built-in functions and user-defined refinements, HELMHOLTZ provides a comprehensive validation solution for Tezos contracts.

Deep Neural Network structures, such as Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental concepts. This study aims to enhance the intuition behind GCNNs by comparing their structure to a traditional signal processing method, matched filtering, demonstrating that the convolutional operation in GCNNs can be viewed as matched filtering in the frequency domain. Furthermore, we illustrate how the GCNN's trainable filter resembles a time-reversed signal of interest, supported by both mathematical and visual evidence, facilitating an intuitive grasp of the GCNN's optimization process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be observed through a Chern-Simons term in its action. The process results in black holes and solitons with rotating properties, and the addition of a magnetic field in the Chern-Simons term affects their mass and charge relationship. The solitons' stability depends on the field's strength. The added magnetic field also enables the formation of charged solitons and black holes in certain conditions. The solitons' mass/charge ratio is compared to that of a scalar field-corrected Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole, and the influence of the magnetic field on this ratio is examined. The added magnetic field, however, disrupts the energy equality between certain solitons and black holes. The process also creates new soliton and black hole structures, such as a rotating, self-correcting Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole with a hairy exterior.

The proposed concept of non-reversible symmetry is explained, along with its underlying theory. Non-reversible symmetry occurs when a reversible transformation meets specific criteria, involving an odd parity matrix that squares to a identity matrix, especially in the context of the Minkowski space. When this happens, the associated brane architecture takes on a distinct form, characterized by the brane's spatial mirror symmetry being broken, resulting in distinct left and right areas. The relationship between non-reversible symmetry and brane architecture is demonstrated through Branes' properties, such as energy density and pressure, which exhibit anisotropy, as well as the non-reversible nature of sound waves. Furthermore, non-reversible symmetry can give rise to branes' anisotrophic expansion and contraction, driven by non-reversible energy transfer between different brane modes.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral measurement. The inferior performance of lateral direction is mainly attributed to the limited spatial resolution aided by the limited lateral field-of-view (FOV) of conventional ultrasound sensors. To overcome this limitation, a novel Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) ultrasound sensor has been introduced. The VSSA sensor possesses several advantages, including enhanced lateral resolution, increased effective lateral FOV, and the capability to operate with lower center frequencies. The simplified design of the VSSA sensor allows for cost-effective fabrication. The performance of the VSSA sensor was compared to the conventional synthetic aperture (CSA) sensor in the field-of-views (FOVs) study. The VSSA sensor exhibited precise displacement measurement capabilities, outperforming the CSA sensor especially in the lateral direction. The study demonstrated that the VSSA sensor achieves optimal measurement results when the width of the illuminated area is doubled its diameter. The findings of the study can be utilized in the design and operation of the VSSA sensor, enabling its use in high-accuracy elastography imaging.

We introduce a new specification language for recursive algorithms, which we call logical pseudocodes, incorporating variables, arrays, and tail recursion. Each logical pseudocode operation is closely linked to a logical statement, which in turn can be verified through established theorem-proving methods. Our approach allows the soundness of an algorithm to be proved and validated, even in the presence of errors or incomplete information, which enables the exploration of key properties such as minimality and optimality.

The concept of a Ramsey character originates from Ramsey theory, indicating the minimal number of colorings required to distinguish a specific pattern in a uniform scenario. This paper explores this idea in the context of Boolean lattices, focusing on V-shaped posets and their Ramsey characteristics. By establishing upper and lower bounds, the study reveals that the Ramsey character of a V-shaped poset with n levels is n+1, for n greater than or equal to two. Additionally, the paper discusses the character of antimajority functions and posets with multiple V-shapes.

In the $k$-centers problem, we are tasked with selecting a subset of $k$ centers that minimizes the maximum distance from any data point to its nearest center. This problem has significant implications in various fields such as machine learning, finance, and biomedical research. We present a novel algorithm, called DASH, for solving the dynamic $k$-centers problem in high-dimensional space. DASH leverages an unusual combination of both adaptive and non-adaptive sampling techniques, ensuring that the maximum distance between centers and data points is closely estimated. We prove that DASH returns a cluster solution no more than twice the optimal number of centers. Moreover, DASH outperforms existing methods by executing in linear time for fixed $k$, while also handling increasing $k$ efficiently. Additionally, we introduce an efficient preprocessing technique for DASH, reducing its time complexity to almost quadratic. In our experiments, DASH consistently demonstrates superior performance compared to alternative methods.

We introduce a novel class of stochastic chaser-eater games on complex structures, where the eater has sight but not mobility, and both players can move freely within these structures. These scenarios represent abstract representations of various real-world situations. Our research establishes concrete hierarchal decompositions for these games, enabling the evaluation of the effectiveness of each player's action across different regions of the structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal payoffs for these games can be calculated by resolving a system of interconnected sub-problems, where each sub-problem corresponds to a distinct state within the overall game framework. These sub-problems are solved concurrently through an algorithm based on dynamic programming, and we have previously shown that this algorithm yields an approximate solution for these games. Building upon this earlier work, we now derive the specific formula for evaluating the effectiveness of each action within each state, and demonstrate that the optimal action for each player can be determined through the comparison of the values obtained from the application of these formulae.

A likelihood function that is in cycles with respect to a group of parameters is analyzed in this paper. We also examine how this property affects nontransitive results, along with the implications for model selection methods.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in restoring regular-dose CT images from low-dose CT scans without labeled training data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because it requires synthesizing two types of images and results in increased memory and computing time. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the generator can efficiently switch between generating high-dose CT images from low-dose CT scans and generating low-dose CT images from high-dose CT scans. We validated the proposed method through comparisons with existing cycleGAN methods and established that it offers superior performance by achieving higher PSNR and SSIM values in multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, our method demonstrates a clear benefit in terms of reduced memory usage and training time without the need for any external techniques.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven dialog understanding tasks on four datasets in China, surpassing current state-of-the-art models like Mulan, MuHan and MuHan-v2 in four out of seven tasks with TelTel-v2 model's scores being particularly notable for significant improvements over baseline models.

This research aims to examine the geometric makeup of an ideal fluid spacetime 
that is expanding, rotating, and subject to various constraints, with certain 
conditions applied. By incorporating a suitable potential function, we derive 
a number of interesting results, including expressions for the conformal Ricci-Yamabe 
metric and soliton in this context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the soliton 
identity is satisfied under certain technical conditions.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across the surface of deformed nuclei. By analyzing the density and momentum distributions, we investigated the structural properties of rotating distorted halo nuclei, specifically $^{42}$Mg, $^{44}$Mg, $^{42}$Si, and $^{44}$Si. These nuclei exhibit inflated sizes and distinct shape decoupling effects in rotational bands, characterized by separation of intrinsic and rotational components and demonstrate how relativistic continuum effects persist across various excitation energies.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to produce non-scalar particles at small angles from the collision direction, a new theoretical framework has been developed to accurately describe this scenario - the Efficient Vector Boson (EVB) approximation. By taking into account the angular dependence of particle behavior, the EVB approach has been found to significantly improve predictions for forward observing facilities, leading to more precise measurements of particle properties. In our research, we expand the limitations of this approximation to internal momenta within particle decay, demonstrating its applicability to a variety of processes and potential future facilities like the Muon Collider Next Generation (μAG) and the Future Circular Electron Positron Collider (FCCee). Through more precise calculations and consistent use of EVB and internal momenta, we expect a 10% improvement in mass measurement accuracy and a 5% gain in energy resolution, which could be as high as 20% for energy dependence.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared representations in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning. By comparing the performance of connected and independent
skill networks, we find that in some scenarios, using separate models for each
task actually outperforms a connected model. To explain this, we show that shared
representations can lead to catastrophic interference, a phenomenon exacerbated
by the use of precise state representations. We also provide a quantitative
analysis of the amount of interference present in different network configurations,
focusing on the effect of state preprocessing. Our research suggests that in
multi-task reinforcement learning using precise state representations, connectivity
does not necessarily induce a benefit in return; instead, further study is
needed on strategies that protect task-specific knowledge when implementing
shared representations.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

In 1933, Kurt Godel and Alonzo Church were actively exchanging letters with J. Barkley Rosser, discussing the possibility of formulating a principle that would allow for the proof of consistency within any formal system. However, Godel passed away in 1975, long before I discovered these historical letters in 2001. Had Godel been alive, I would have liked to discuss his thoughts on this matter, as his opinions would have been incredibly valuable. Throughout this paper, I will examine the concepts that arose from Godel's influence, including his incompleteness theorems, Ullian truths, and the concept of a consistent formal system, as well as the opinions of other logicians with whom I have had the opportunity to converse.

This paper formulates the three balls conjecture in terms of monogenic functions, which are essentially the complex analytic equivalents in hyperspace to harmonic functions in real space. We then prove this conjecture for functions that are part of a specific whole function within the algebra ${\cal N}^3(1)$ over three-dimensional space. Additionally, we explore related conclusions for functions within this algebra's derived series.

When overseeing a vast expensive dataset, selective sampling is a common strategy to speed up the process of finding a specific pattern. The basic method of selective sampling involves strategically choosing a new sample based on the information gained from previous selections. The standard approach extends this concept to cases with multiple samples. However, when dealing with inequalities in data availability, standard selective sampling techniques can be biased in their outcomes. To address this issue, we propose a novel sequential selective sampling algorithm that ensures equality in data accessibility. The algorithm operates under minimal assumptions concerning the dataset and pattern, and we establish theoretical bounds for its performance.
